articles.title: Unpacking Indonesia With Marcus Tantau
articles.full_text:
The country is currently beset by wildfires, political ructions, and intensifying economic troubles.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto (center) salutes during a parade marking Bhayangkara Day, the anniversary of the founding of the Indonesian National Police, in Bogor, West Java, Indonesia, July 1, 2026.
Marcus Tantau is a senior associate at Templeton Research with a focus on Indonesia, which is beset by El Nino-fueled wildfires, political ructions amid a cabinet reshuffle, and confusing signals over the economy.
This month’s reshuffle was the biggest since President Prabowo Subianto took power two years ago and Tantau says the Indonesian leader is clearly focused on shoring-up support ahead the next election, which is not due until 2029.
The reshuffle also sidelined supporters of former president Joko Widodo, who helped Prabowo win the vote in 2024. It came amid intense speculation regarding the state of the country’s finances and its efforts to combat the wildfires, which politicians are attempting to justify.
But arguments that food security and rice production justify the burning-off and clearing of land remain out of step with the region, where climate change and this year’s El Nino weather phenomena are taking a heavy toll.
“The mood towards Prabowo isn’t that great,” Tantau said. “It’s all these issues, around job security. The rupiah has declined significantly since Prabowo came to power. It’s all of these issues that are linked to one another.
“But I think Prabowo is mostly focused on improving or consolidating his political hold on Indonesia. And we saw that recently with the cabinet shuffle where he was, for all intents and purposes, sidelining Joko appointees.”
Tantau also publishes the Substack newsletter “Five Things You Should Know About Indonesia.”

articles.title: Professor S.I. Keethaponcalan on Two Years of the AKD Presidency in Sri Lanka
articles.full_text:
“The NPP government made a sensible decision to accept and continue most of the economic policies and programs Ranil Wickremesinghe introduced.”
Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake
It is a little over two years since Anura Kumara Dissanayake, or AKD as he is popularly known, was elected Sri Lanka’s ninth executive president. His victory was an unambiguous vote for change. Unlike his predecessors, AKD did not belong to a political dynasty, nor did he hail from an elite background. Seven weeks after he took over the reins as president, AKD’s National People’s Power (NPP), a coalition of leftist parties, won an emphatic victory in general elections, not only securing a two-thirds majority in parliament but also performing well in the Tamil-dominated Northern Province. Understandably, expectations for AKD ran high.
So how has his government performed? In a discussion with Sudha Ramachandran, South Asia editor of The Diplomat, Professor Soosaipillai I. Keethaponcalan, former chair of the Conflict Analysis and Dispute Resolution Department at Salisbury University in Maryland, said that while AKD has done a “commendable job” on the economic front and has sought to prosecute corrupt politicians, he has done “very little, if anything” in finding a political solution to the ethnic conflict. “There have been no significant prosecutions of those responsible for wartime atrocities,” he said.
Besides, the AKD government has taken no steps towards revoking the executive presidency — a key election campaign pledge. “Like many of its predecessors, [the AKD government] may have come to appreciate the extensive powers of the executive presidency and may believe that these powers are necessary for political stability,” Keethaponcalan said.
Although Anura Kumara Dissanayake and the NPP were at the forefront of the criticism of Ranil Wickremesinghe’s debt restructuring strategy, as president he followed the same strategy to satisfy IMF norms. How different has his presidency been from that of his predecessors?
I used to believe that in Sri Lanka, two entities were firmly committed to their ideological positions and goals. One was the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), and the other was the Janata Vimukti Peramuna (JVP). The LTTE perished partly because of its unwavering commitment to the cause of Tamil Eelam. However, I have been surprised by how adaptive and flexible the JVP has become in its ideological positions over the last two years. The party, which forms the core of the NPP government, has demonstrated remarkable flexibility in responding to current realities and political compulsions.
The JVP launched two unsuccessful armed rebellions to establish a socialist state in Sri Lanka. Given this history, I was surprised to see how readily the party moved away from its socialist ideology after coming to power. Its dramatic shift in its traditionally anti-Indian position is another example of this ideological flexibility.
Similarly, while in opposition, the JVP strongly resisted Ranil Wickremesinghe’s strategy of securing an IMF bailout and implementing the associated economic restructuring program. However, once in power, the party appears to have recognized the importance of the IMF program and has continued with essentially the same strategy. The current IMF program is scheduled to expire in March 2027, and I would not be surprised if the NPP government sought a new agreement with the IMF. Such a decision would further demonstrate the remarkable transformation of the JVP’s economic policy orientation.
However, I see some differences, particularly the government’s apparent determination to prosecute former political leaders accused of corruption and other malpractices. During his presidency, Wickremesinghe failed to adequately address corruption, one of the major grievances highlighted by the Aragalaya (“struggle” in Sinhala) — the mass protests in 2022 that toppled the Gotabaya Rajapaksa government and created the political circumstances that eventually brought him to power.
Nevertheless, in my view, the incumbent NPP government has largely continued the policies of its predecessors, particularly those pursued by Wickremesinghe. The most striking change, therefore, is not in the direction of government policy but in the JVP’s willingness to abandon or modify positions it had defended for decades.
AKD had promised to abolish the executive presidency. He has the numbers in parliament to push through constitutional change. So why hasn’t he acted?
Sri Lanka has had, and continues to have, a political movement advocating the abolition of the executive presidential system and the restoration of a parliamentary form of government. Traditionally, the JVP, including President Dissanayake as one of its leaders, played a pivotal role in this movement. That is precisely why the party promised to abolish the executive presidency in its 2024 election manifesto.
As you know, the NPP secured a comfortable majority of more than two-thirds in parliament. Yet it has taken no significant steps toward constitutional reform. Instead, in September 2026, it amended the constitution to increase the retirement age of Supreme Court judges — a relatively minor and, in my view, unnecessary change.
Consequently, two years after Dissanayake came to power, the constitution introduced by the JVP’s former arch-enemy, President J. R. Jayewardene, remains largely intact. I doubt that the NPP government will demonstrate much enthusiasm for constitutional reform in the near future.
I see two possible reasons for this reluctance. First, the NPP government, like many of its predecessors, may have come to appreciate the extensive powers of the executive presidency and may believe that these powers are necessary for political stability. Second, initiating a comprehensive constitutional reform process could force the government to confront several politically uncomfortable questions. One such question concerns the future of the provincial council system, which the JVP vehemently opposed in the past. Should the system be retained, reformed, or abolished? Any of these choices could create political difficulties for the government.
What steps has AKD taken with regard to finding a political solution to Tamil grievances?
Very little, if anything. Traditionally, the JVP, like many Sinhala nationalist organizations, did not recognize the existence of an ethnic conflict in Sri Lanka or acknowledge that Tamils faced grievances specific to their community. Instead, the party viewed Sri Lanka’s problem primarily as one of terrorism. Therefore, I am not surprised that the NPP government has shown little interest in pursuing a political solution to Tamil grievances. There has been no meaningful dialogue with Tamil political leaders specifically aimed at finding such a solution.
In his 2024 election manifesto, Dissanayake promised to hold the long-delayed provincial council elections. That promise remains unfulfilled. This is particularly significant because the NPP won parliamentary seats in the Jaffna district in 2024, with Tamil voters electing JVP-affiliated candidates in a remarkable departure from traditional voting patterns.
I do not necessarily believe that the government’s reluctance to hold provincial council elections is motivated by racism or ethnic discrimination. Rather, I suspect that the government is uncomfortable facing voters at this juncture because its political appeal appears to be eroding.
Interestingly, I do not see much public pressure from the Tamil community over the continued postponement of provincial council elections. The major Tamil political parties have also failed to make this issue a significant central political demand. Consequently, the government faces little sustained pressure to address the Tamil question through meaningful political negotiations or constitutional reform.
How would you rate this government’s performance in bringing to justice those who carried out horrific crimes, even atrocities, against the Tamils during the civil war?
Not encouraging. The government has yet to meet many of the demands made through the United Nations Human Rights Council processes in Geneva. Nor has it introduced significant new initiatives to address the grievances of the victims. Families of those who disappeared during the final phase of the war continue their protests and campaigns demanding justice. To my knowledge, there have been no significant prosecutions of those responsible for wartime atrocities.
For example, more human remains have recently been recovered from the Chemmani mass graves in Jaffna, where hundreds of individuals are believed to have been buried. Yet the government has not established a systematic, adequately empowered mechanism to investigate such crimes and ensure accountability.
In Sri Lanka, regardless of who is in power, investigating and prosecuting war-related crimes, particularly those allegedly committed by members of the armed forces, is politically extremely difficult. Such a move could amount to political suicide for any government. Therefore, I have little hope that the families of those who disappeared or were killed during the civil war will receive the justice they have been demanding for so long.
How is the Sri Lankan economy doing under President Dissanayake?
I think the NPP government has done a commendable job on this front. However, the credit for pulling Sri Lanka out of the 2022 economic crisis and restoring some economic stability should go primarily to Wickremesinghe. The NPP government made a sensible decision to accept and continue most of the economic policies and programs Wickremesinghe introduced. That strategy has worked, and Sri Lanka’s economy remains relatively stable.
The NPP government has also made its own progress. For example, Sri Lanka’s foreign reserves increased from approximately US$4.5 billion in 2023 to around US$7 billion in August 2026. This is a significant achievement.
Nevertheless, I believe a more meaningful assessment of the government’s economic performance can be made after the current IMF bailout program expires in March 2027. How the government manages the economy beyond the current IMF arrangement will be a crucial test of its economic policies.
There are plans to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979 with new anti-terrorism legislation. Does Sri Lanka have a terrorism problem today?
articles.summary: “The NPP government made a sensible decision to accept and continue most of the economic policies and programs Ranil Wickremesinghe introduced.”

articles.title: How the Fossil Fuel Industry ‘Captured’ Australia and Maintains Its Political Dominance
articles.full_text:
By framing coal and gas as essential to jobs, prosperity and national identity, the industry continues to resist the transition to renewable energy.
As public concern over worsening climate change grows, Australia’s fossil fuel industry has been asserting that coal and gas are central to technological innovation and economic security.
Australia is one of the world’s largest exporters of coal and gas and has among the world’s highest per capita carbon emissions. As a leading “petrostate,” it is perhaps unsurprising that the fossil fuel sector has been central in shaping the nation’s energy and climate policies.
The political capture of Australia by the fossil fuel industries has stymied any meaningful attempt to move away from fossil energy. They have historically obstructed attempts to regulate and reduce carbon emissions through lobbying, networking, and financial donations to parties in the political arena. The end game is to promote fossil energy to the public as essential to the past, present, and future of Australian society; what can be termed a form of “carbon populism.” 
Unpicking this complex web of political influence is essential if meaningful decarbonization is to be achieved.
The outsized political influence of the fossil fuel industries in Australia has a long history. As former political staffer Guy Pearse noted in his book “High and Dry,” the so-called “greenhouse mafia” of corporate executives and lobbyists played a key role in the years of the Howard government (1996-2007) in shaping the rejection of climate and emissions regulation. That defensive political activity continued in the campaigns against carbon pricing under the Rudd and Gillard Labor governments (2007-2013) and the following nine years of conservative rule. Indeed, under the current Albanese Labor government (2022-present) fossil fuel interests in gas and coal continue to have significant influence over energy and climate policy.
This influence has been achieved through various practices, such as lobbying, networking, and industry association representation. This has involved direct representations by corporate executives and paid lobbyists to senior government ministers and bureaucrats or more informal interactions in the halls of parliament. Here, coal and gas representatives stress their role as creators of public value through employment, revenue for public coffers and broader economic growth. Financial donations have further amplified political influence, with fossil fuel corporations donating close to AU$4 million to Australia’s major political parties during 2024-25 which included the last Federal Election.
The blurring divide between politics and the fossil fuel industry is particularly evident in the social embeddedness of industry representatives and executives within the political sphere. This involves personal and professional relationships. A common theme here has been the concept of a “revolving door” between industry and government. For example, several reports have listed the career trajectories of retiring politicians and bureaucrats as they move into senior industry and consulting roles, as well as industry representatives taking up political advisory appointments. This inter-connectedness of industry and politics has included both major political parties, highlighting a strong capital-state nexus that is committed to the continued expansion of fossil energy resources.
This close “understanding” between different levels of government and the fossil fuel sector is often explicitly highlighted in the public statements of politicians expressing their loyalty to the resources sector. Here, politicians depict the industry as the backbone of the Australian success story and deserving of a seat at the table. Examples have included: advocating for the appointment of a former resources minister to chair a peak mining industry association; the federal treasurer displaying a lump of coal in the parliament and declaring its national benefits; and a former minister for resources posting a heartfelt note of farewell to the Australian mining sector on Facebook. As one interviewee in our research acknowledged: “Yes, there is a revolving door of consultants and management personnel between ministerial offices and industry groups, and companies. There always has been!”
More broadly, the fossil fuel industry has been central to the shaping of public attitudes and understandings of economic development and national identity. For instance, as the CEO of coal giant Peabody Energy declared in promoting the continued expansion of the Australian coal industry: “Coal has transformed society over hundreds of years by fueling industrial revolutions and digital economies. It’s the pride of Australia’s past, and the pride of its future.”
In its public relations, the industry has sought to bring together a range of discourses on how coal and gas underpins the collective welfare of Australia. This has included arguments about the role of coal-fired power in providing cheap and reliable electricity, the economic contribution of export earnings and mining royalties, and employment and job creation. For instance, many of the industry’s public statements have for years stressed the way in which fossil fuel extraction is one of the nation’s highest export earners and contributes to the collective good through mining royalties and tax revenue which contribute to the provision of essential government services.
Despite being highly capital intensive, coal mining has also been presented as a major source of employment, emphasizing its role in regional development and as a key part of many communities. This focus on local communities, job creation, and regional development has been reinforced through the industry’s advertising and community programs, showcasing local conservation and sustainability programs, profiles of mine workers and their family lives, sponsorship of local sporting teams and schools and hospitals, Indigenous employment programs, and “education” programs promoting the benefits of fossil fuel energy. As critics have noted, these practices act as a form of “inoculation PR” aimed at defusing more negative perceptions of the industry and winning over the hearts and minds of local communities and the general public to the worthiness of fossil fuel extraction.
The Magical Thinking of a Fossil-fueled Future
In a context of growing public concern over worsening climate change, the fossil fuel industry has sought to highlight its current benefits and also project an image of the future in which it continues to grow. Despite the rapidly declining cost of renewable energy and growing global moves towards decarbonization, the coal and gas industries and aligned politicians have sought to promote a “fossil fuels forever” imaginary.
This has involved asserting the central role of coal and gas in the economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as technological innovation and the need for energy security. Examples have included the framing of Australia’s export gas industry as a “transition fuel” in contributing to global emissions reductions, as well as the coal industry’s on-going promotion of so-called “clean coal” via phantom technologies such as carbon capture and storage. In response, state and federal politicians have continued to talk up the future of fossil energy, and new coal and gas projects continue to be green-lit.
Despite decades of political debate over climate and energy policy, Australia’s role as a major fossil energy producer remains unchanged. As current and future generations watch a world unravelling under the weight of ever worsening climate disruption, the legacy of the fossil-fuel industry’s outsized influence on the failure to decarbonize weighs heavily.

articles.title: Behind the Veil of Religious Harmony in Cambodia
articles.full_text:
Aggregate rankings mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine tolerance.
On paper, Cambodia often appears as a site of religious tolerance, boasting favorable scores in global indices that measure selected elements of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB). Over the years, these “rankings” have manufactured a facade of harmony that masks realities on the ground. State influence over Buddhist institutions, structural inequalities, and the quiet marginalization of minority groups and the destruction of Indigenous sacred places are routinely obscured by aggregate rankings that mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine harmony.
This gap in analysis is the central focus of Asia Centre’s report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings,” published on September 28. At its core, the report interrogates what standard metrics capture and, more importantly, what they deliberately or inadvertently leave out.
Several existing reports provide valuable insights into Cambodia’s Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) landscape. The Pew Research Center’s Government Restrictions Index and Social Hostilities Index both offer comparative global measurements of religious freedom and tolerance. In 2023, Cambodia scored 5 out of 10 on the Government Restrictions Index and 0.2 out of 10 on the Social Hostilities Index, indicating relatively favorable performance compared with its neighboring countries. 
The U.S. Department of State’s International Religious Freedom Reports provide detailed annual documentation of government policies and religious-freedom conditions. Its 2023 report on Cambodia identified several areas of concern, including state influence over Buddhist institutions and monks’ political affiliations, Muslim representation in local government leadership, and Indigenous Peoples’ land rights. 
The report “Diving Deep into Cambodia’s FoRB: An Exploration of Community Hopes and Collective Hurdles” (2024), produced by Women Peace Makers in collaboration with Danmission Cambodia, offers insights into the experiences of different ethno-religious communities in Cambodia, particularly regarding religious education, participation in religious leadership, and access to sacred sites.
Asia Centre’s report builds on this research by examining the institutional relationships. Our report draws attention to power structures that shape how religious freedom is exercised and protected in practice. It also considers developments since 2024, including the leadership transition and the Cambodia-Thailand border conflict. Drawing on the latest cases and consultations with experts and affected communities, the report goes beyond aggregate rankings to examine the political, institutional, and structural conditions underlying Cambodia’s FoRB landscape.
Four findings are particularly significant. First, Cambodia’s appearance of religious harmony obscures the structural inequalities. Existing research pays limited attention to tensions and hostilities between religious communities, particularly between majority and minority groups. This risks mistaking silence and the absence of overt conflict for “harmony.” Asia Centre’s findings instead suggest that “harmony” is a by-product of state influence, structural inequalities and fear that constrain religious expression. By examining these underlying conditions, the report brings greater visibility to grievances and experiences that may otherwise remain unspoken.
Second, state influence over religious institutions constrains religious autonomy and serves political objectives. Buddhism’s central role in Cambodian national identity makes this relationship particularly significant: political influence over Buddhist institutions can shape not only religious expression but also political expression. Institutional and material pressures discourage Buddhist monks from challenging state expectations, while political actors mobilize religious authority to legitimize government objectives, including during the 2025 Cambodia–Thailand border conflict. By examining these dynamics, the report highlights the often-overlooked links between religion and political power.
Third, the intersectionality of rights is obscured. Existing human rights reporting frequently treats religious discrimination, restrictions on fundamental freedoms, and Indigenous land dispossession as separate issues. Asia Centre connects these concerns through a FoRB lens, showing how development projects and land concessions that destroy Indigenous sacred sites can undermine communities’ ability to sustain their religious and cultural practices, while raising broader questions about equal access to institutional protection and accountability.
Fourth, limited FoRB literacy prevents government officials, civil society, independent media, and even some faith-based organizations from recognizing violations. Hence, unequal treatment in administrative procedures, inadequate protection against prejudices, or absences of effective remedies for affected communities are ignored. Asia Centre’s report highlights the need to strengthen FoRB literacy among these stakeholders to ensure that they have the capacity to correctly identify violations, report them, and make sure remedial actions are taken. 
Building on these stakeholder capacities, ultimately Asia Centre’s report moves beyond aggregate global indices to expose the institutional and political mechanisms shaping Cambodia’s actual religious landscape. 
By examining state influence over Buddhist institutions, the intersectionality of rights, and the systemic challenges faced by minorities and Indigenous communities, the report provides a comprehensive country-level analysis. Its recommendations translate these insights into concrete responsibilities for the Cambodian government, civil society, international organizations, independent media, and faith-based groups. 
Rather than treating Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) as an isolated concern, the report connects it to broader social and political dimensions, offering practical guidelines to bridge the gap between formal legal protections and lived realities in Cambodia.
This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings.” Download the full report here. For more information about Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org.

Asia Centre connects these concerns through a FoRB lens, showing how development projects and land concessions that destroy Indigenous sacred sites can undermine communities’ ability to sustain their religious and cultural practices, while raising broader questions about equal access to institutional protection and accountability.
Fourth, limited FoRB literacy prevents government officials, civil society, independent media, and even some faith-based organizations from recognizing violations. Hence, unequal treatment in administrative procedures, inadequate protection against prejudices, or absences of effective remedies for affected communities are ignored. Asia Centre’s report highlights the need to strengthen FoRB literacy among these stakeholders to ensure that they have the capacity to correctly identify violations, report them, and make sure remedial actions are taken. 
Building on these stakeholder capacities, ultimately Asia Centre’s report moves beyond aggregate global indices to expose the institutional and political mechanisms shaping Cambodia’s actual religious landscape. 
By examining state influence over Buddhist institutions, the intersectionality of rights, and the systemic challenges faced by minorities and Indigenous communities, the report provides a comprehensive country-level analysis. Its recommendations translate these insights into concrete responsibilities for the Cambodian government, civil society, international organizations, independent media, and faith-based groups. 
Rather than treating Freedom of Religion or Belief (FoRB) as an isolated concern, the report connects it to broader social and political dimensions, offering practical guidelines to bridge the gap between formal legal protections and lived realities in Cambodia.
This op-ed is based on Asia Centre’s new report, “Religious Freedom in Cambodia: Unpacking the Rankings.” Download the full report here. For more information about Asia Centre, visit asiacentre.org. 
On paper, Cambodia often appears as a site of religious tolerance, boasting favorable scores in global indices that measure selected elements of freedom of religion or belief (FoRB). Over the years, these “rankings” have manufactured a facade of harmony that masks realities on the ground. State influence over Buddhist institutions, structural inequalities, and the quiet marginalization of minority groups and the destruction of Indigenous sacred places are routinely obscured by aggregate rankings that mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine harmony.
articles.summary: Aggregate rankings mistake the absence of overt conflict and the fear of speaking up for genuine tolerance.

articles.title: Hindutva Goons Unleash Violence on Anti-Modi Protesters
articles.full_text:
Activists of the Hindu Raksha Dal, an outfit that furthers the Sangh Parivar’s agenda, were caught on camera beating students and youth participating in the Delhi protests.
A screenshot of a News Capsule video showing Hindu Raksha Dal activists assaulting young women and men at the anti-government protests in New Delhi, India, Oct.10, 2026.
In recent weeks, New Delhi and other Indian cities have witnessed massive anti-government demonstrations and flash protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, over allegations of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
To prevent students and youth from gathering, the BJP government has used intimidation and force. In addition to arresting protesters, it has heavily barricaded roads, shut down metro stations, and deployed tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, including the Delhi Police, Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force, Indo-Tibetan Border Police, and Sashastra Seema Bal.
Several of these forces are normally deployed along India’s borders or in insurgency-wracked regions. For example, the CRPF companies deployed in the Delhi protests were shifted from former Maoist strongholds in Chhattisgarh and parts of militancy-hit Jammu and Kashmir. In Delhi, these paramilitary forces are being used against unarmed youth activists of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the All India Students’ Association, and other leftist organizations.
What makes the government’s crackdown particularly reprehensible is that un-uniformed men are being allowed to assault the protesters. These are not isolated incidents; several young women and men have come forward with horrifying accounts of the violence they faced at the hands of these thugs.
Importantly, these men are unleashing violence in full view of the police. They have the blessings of the ruling dispensation.
Photographs and videos circulating on social media show men sporting saffron scarves — saffron is the color of the Sangh Parivar, a family of Hindutva-espousing organizations, of which the BJP is a part — shouting slogans in support of the Narendra Modi government, chasing young men and women, dragging them and beating them up mercilessly with sticks. They are brazen about their violence, describing their victims as “anti-national elements” who “deserve to be thrashed.”
“Delhi Police tum lath bajao, hum tumhare saath hain” (Delhi Police, you wield the baton, we are with you), they chant, egging on the police to beat the protesters.
The police and paramilitary personnel in whose presence the vigilantes acted took no action to force them off the streets. None of them was packed into police vans the way unarmed students were dragged and pushed into buses.
A video filmed during the crackdown on October 10 in central Delhi showed goons beating up young men and women, even minors. When a woman intervened on a male victim’s behalf, the goons can be seen falling upon her, pushing her to the ground, and pulling at her clothes. All this was done in the presence of at least one policeman. The footage showed a policeman eventually intervening, but he did so not to stop the assault or restrain the assailant and detain him, but to lead him away rather gently.
The video triggered anger and outrage in India, forcing the police to eventually detain four men — Raman Saini, Vivekanand alias Vivek, Kapil Kumar, and Ravinder Singh alias Govind Hindu — of the Hindu Raksha Dal (HRD) or Hindu Protection Organization.
Admitting that the four were members of his organization, HRD chief Bhupendra Singh Tomar aka Pinky Bhaiyya described them as “warriors” who were “working for Sanatan Dharma” (literally, universal truth i.e., Hinduism). In an interview with Outlook magazine, Tomar justified the violence they unleashed at the October 10 protests. The CJP activists “tried to vitiate the atmosphere in the country” during the protests at Jantar Mantar in July. “We will deal with these people who are resorting to violence, and we will set them straight. We take pride in our actions, and we will continue to do so,” Tomar said.
Founded in 2013, the Hindu Raksha Dal is among dozens of vigilante groups that have mushroomed under Modi’s rule. They have thrived under the Sangh Parivar’s patronage. Their activists cannot be dismissed as mere street gangs. They are the Sangh Parivar’s foot soldiers and unleash violence to further its Hindutva agenda. Outfits like the HRD and the Bharatiya Gau Raksha Dal (Indian Cow Protection Organization) freely engage in violence as they enjoy state protection.
HRD activists are rarely convicted or punished. Saini, Vivek, Kumar, and Singh were caught on video and were arrested under public pressure, but they were freed on bail soon after. Delhi Police did not raise objections to their release by the courts. On their release, Tomar was there to welcome and garland the four men.
Tomar himself has over 30 cases against him for hate speech, distributing weapons, issuing death threats, damaging property, assault, extortion, and raising inflammatory slogans. The list of complaints and cases against him is long. He has been arrested in a few cases only to be let off on bail soon after. His supporters have an apt slogan to describe this: “Aaj jail, kal bail, aur phir wahi khel” (jail today, bail tomorrow and then again, the same game).
The HRD has carried out dozens of attacks on Muslims, secular Indians, and the BJP’s critics. In 2020, Tomar claimed credit for the attack on students at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in New Delhi. “JNU is a hotbed of anti-national activities and we cannot tolerate this,” he said, taking “full responsibility” for the violence that left at least 30 people, including teachers and students, injured.
In August 2024, HRD activists burnt down houses and property of Muslims in a slum in Ghaziabad, claiming that they were Bangladeshis living illegally in India. In December 2025, Tomar and his son were arrested for distributing swords in Ghaziabad for the “self-defense” of Hindus.
Outfits like the HRD enable the Sangh Parivar and the BJP government to not only freely unleash illegitimate violence but also deny their links to the perpetrators of such violence. The membership of Sangh Parivar outfits and their fellow travelers is nebulous. Consequently, it is hard to pin such violence on the Modi government.

articles.title: Amid Economic Challenges, China Turns to Vulnerable Workforce to Fix Its Social Security Problems
articles.full_text:
China is looking to “optimize and enhance” its social security program. People fear that will translate to pressure on gig economy workers and rural migrant workers.
“It is critical that we utilize data to identify individuals who have not contributed to the social security program. Currently, some people have not participated in the program, but we will use different means to identify and find them to encourage them to join.” These are quotes from Li Zhong, deputy minister of the Chinese Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS), on the government’s goal to increase the number of individuals in the Chinese social security program. 
Li’s remarks at the ministry’s news conference on October 10 quickly gained the public’s attention. Using digital technology to identify individuals is one of multiple measures announced by the MOHRSS toward its goal to “optimize and enhance” the sustainability, fairness, security, convenience, and standardization of the Chinese social security program. The Chinese government will encourage gig economy workers, rural migrant workers, and individuals in new forms of employment to join state-managed pension plans. On the corporate side, the government will focus on small and mid-size businesses and social groups to increase its pool of social security funds.
With low birth rates and high retirement numbers in the coming years, the Chinese social security program is under increasing stress. Warning signs began emerging as early as 2014. According to predictions from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS) in April 2019, the Chinese pension plan could see a funding deficit by 2028. The financial gap could jump to 11.28 trillion yuan by 2050 – or 16.73 trillion yuan in a scenario without government financial assistance. 
At the rate CASS projected seven years ago, the Chinese state pension plan will see its funds depleted by 2035. Given that the Chinese economy is facing continuous challenges in its post-COVID recovery, the Chinese state pension plan is likely facing a worse scenario than researchers predicted back in 2019. 
The Chinese government has already taken steps such as increasing the basic social security deduction to maintain contribution inflow. China has also implemented a gradual delay in the retirement age since January 2025. Starting in September 2025, the Chinese government announced plans to force businesses to contribute to social security funds. Now Li’s comments have raised speculation that MOHRSS will use data-tracking tools to force individuals to join the pension scheme as well. 
However, in a deteriorating economy, both employers and employees show little faith in the state-managed social security program. Businesses view this as a substantial cost that could lead to shutdowns, and employees view the mandatory contribution as a significant reduction of their disposable income. Younger Chinese workers have doubts about the likelihood of them getting the contributions back in the form of payments when they reach retirement age. 
In the first quarter of 2026, approximately 58 million individuals paused their social security contributions. In some regions, banks and local governments have started low-interest loan products to encourage individuals to contribute to the social security program amid financial difficulties.
For low-income individuals, pension plan deductions become an additional burden because of the continuously increasing minimum contribution base. For example, in Shanghai, a job with a monthly salary of 7,546 yuan or less would require the employer and the employee to contribute a combined minimum of 2,712 yuan each month. But, the monthly minimum salary in Shanghai is just 2,740 yuan. As a result, the social security contribution ratio could reach as high as 98.9 percent to hire a minimum-salary worker.  
Facing pressure to maintain the employment rate and address youth unemployment, the Chinese government decided to target its “flexible employment” population, who rely on the gig economy to survive in China’s post-COVID economic downturn. Research from the Chinese Academy of Labor and Social Security indicates that 34.9 percent of China’s 200 million gig economy workers participated in the social security program, far lower than the 95 percent participation rate set by the MOHRSS. Media reports also predict that the flexible employment population could reach 320 million in 2026. That suggests the social security gap will grow even larger as the Chinese economy creates fewer high-paying, stable jobs. 
With a struggling economy and a challenging employment market, the Chinese government needs solutions to maintain the financial contributions to its social security program. Yet targeting individuals already facing significant challenges in flexible employment is unlikely to lead to positive results.

articles.title: What the New China-North Korea Bridge Really Means
articles.full_text:
12 years after construction finished, the New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. Will North Korea’s economy open too?
This photo from North Korean state media shows the New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea on the day of its official ribbon-cutting ceremony, Oct. 15, 2026.
The New Yalu River Bridge, which links Dandong in China’s Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Pyongan province, has finally opened, a full 12 years after construction finished in 2014. The two countries held an opening ceremony on October 15 and began running cargo trucks across the bridge, which is known as the Amnok River bridge in North Korea.
For years the bridge symbolized China-North Korea economic cooperation and also the practical limits on how far that cooperation could actually go. Now it is finally doing the job it was built for.
The two countries agreed to build the bridge in 2009, and construction began the following year. It was a major project meant to get past the logistical limits of the existing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge. A four-lane bridge more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) long could greatly expand the flow of goods between Dandong and Sinuiju. China was willing to pay for construction to open a new channel for economic cooperation with the North.
Fifteen years ago, I was reporting for Daily NK in China. Back then, Dandong was full of anticipation about the bridge. People everywhere said a new crossing would bring a surge in China-North Korea trade, and that a new economic zone would grow up around Sinuiju and Dandong. Chinese businesspeople expected trade with the North to expand, and property prices near the planned development areas began to climb.
In August 2011, Daily NK reported that work on a pontoon bridge for the construction was 70 percent complete and that nearby real estate prices were rising. Some in Dandong even speculated that the bridge might lead North Korea to open its economy more widely. I still remember that mood clearly from my time on the ground.
Reality fell short of those hopes. The bridge was finished in 2014, but the North Korean side never properly built the connecting roads or customs facilities. Ups and downs in bilateral relations, international sanctions, and the COVID-19 border closure followed, and the bridge stayed shut for years. It was a long wait for the Chinese businesspeople who had hoped for new opportunities, and for everyone who had expected trade with the North to grow.
North Korea’s insularity alone doesn’t explain the delay. The two countries’ economic interests, the political climate, sanctions, and other factors all played a part. What is clear, though, is that North Korean authorities took a long and cautious approach to how much economic contact with the outside world they would allow, and how they would manage it.
In the end, the hard part was not building the bridge. It was getting past the North Korean authorities’ extremely narrow threshold. Pyongyang wanted the economic benefits, but it never let down its guard against the changes outside contact might bring. The 12 years the bridge sat effectively unused lay bare this contradiction at the heart of the North Korean economy.
More Trade Means New Opportunities and New Tests
So now that the bridge is open, will North Korea’s economy change? In the short term, we can expect more trade and more efficient transport between the two countries. Freight that used to pile onto the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge can now be spread out, and there is finally a route that can reliably carry larger volumes of goods.
Still, it would be a mistake to assume the opening will quickly produce a jump in trade or better lives for ordinary North Koreans. How much actually moves will depend on customs procedures, transport costs, trade permits, and how goods are distributed inside North Korea. A wider bridge does not necessarily mean North Korea’s economy has opened any wider.
The bigger story may be how distribution inside North Korea changes. Markets are still central to how ordinary North Koreans make a living. Lately, however, the authorities have not simply been suppressing the general markets. They have been using state-run stores, state grain shops, and other retail outlets to expand state control over distribution and sales.
Under these conditions, if more imports flow across the bridge, state-approved trading companies and distribution agencies are likely to benefit first. In the past, private merchants brought in imported goods through various channels and supplied them to markets. That model may give way further to one where the state manages the import and allocation of goods, with markets and retail outlets operating beneath it.
Private merchants could still find new openings. More stable logistics and a larger supply of Chinese consumer goods and raw materials could mean more choice for shoppers and steadier prices for some items. If factories and enterprises can source raw materials more easily, production could benefit too.
But if the state tightens its grip on imports and distribution, the gains could concentrate in the agencies that hold trade permits and the power to allocate goods. Private merchants would become more dependent on state-designated distribution channels, and the various costs and informal payments they face could well rise.
How the bridge ties into North Korea’s “20×10” regional development policy is also worth watching. The North is racing to build local industrial factories, but putting up a building is one thing and running a factory is another. What matters is not how many factories have been built. It is how many days a month they actually run, where their raw materials come from, and what prices residents pay for what they produce. Without a steady supply of raw materials, electricity, and production equipment, these factories will struggle to operate.
Here, more Chinese raw materials and supplies could improve operating conditions at some local factories. Yet the more these factories rely on Chinese inputs, the further they drift from the self-reliant local economy the authorities keep promoting. 
Development around Sinuiju also deserves attention. According to a recent Daily NK investigation, North Korea has reportedly pitched Chinese businesspeople on a plan to develop the area behind the bridge and some 40 square kilometers (15 square miles) of southern Sinuiju into an economic hub for logistics, processing, trade, and commerce. This suggests Pyongyang wants to use the bridge’s opening to make more economic use of the border region.
We should still separate development plans from actual investment and production. Current United Nations sanctions sharply restrict imports of industrial equipment, exports of North Korean processed goods, and joint ventures. Early on, the benefits will likely be limited to better customs and logistics, with any large-scale industrial cooperation moving slowly.
Above all, North Korea’s economy could become even more dependent on China. Deeper reliance on Chinese raw materials, consumer goods, capital, and logistics networks might give the economy a short-term lift. It could also leave the economy more exposed to shifts in Chinese policy and trade conditions. The gap between the self-reliance the regime preaches and its real dependence on China could grow wider.
Ultimately, the bridge’s opening is both an opportunity and a major test for North Korea’s economy. The question is what the authorities do with the extra goods and economic openings. Will they let ordinary people expand their economic activity, or will the state tighten its hold on profits and distribution channels? The answer looks set to shape the structure of North Korea’s economy in the years ahead.
The number of trucks crossing the bridge is not the only thing to watch. Actual freight volumes, the goods being traded, customs procedures, and shipping costs all matter. But to really judge how North Korea’s economy is changing, we need to follow where those goods go, who controls the trade, and how it ultimately affects people’s daily lives.
That means tracking specific economic indicators over time. How many trucks cross the bridge each month? How much does the share of Chinese goods in markets change? How are people’s purchases split between state-run outlets and the general markets, and how is that changing?
We also need to look at how many days local factories with more Chinese inputs actually run and how much they produce, and how more imports affect consumer prices and people’s purchasing power.
With these questions in mind, the Daily NK sees a need to keep tracking changes in North Korea’s economic structure and in people’s living conditions. Comparing trends at three months, six months, and one year after the opening should give a clearer picture of how the economy is really changing.
What matters here is the direction of change, not whether a single number rises or falls. If imports go up but purchasing power doesn’t improve, we need to find out why. If state stores see more customers, we need to know whether private market trade is shrinking or whether both are growing. More goods coming in and people finding it easier to buy things are two very different matters.
In particular, comparing economic conditions in major cities such as Sinuiju (North Pyongan province), Pyongsong (South Pyongan province), and Hyesan (Ryanggang province) can show whether more border trade is reaching people inland and in the provinces. Even if imports grow at the border, distribution costs and local supply conditions mean residents in different areas may feel the change very differently.
We also need to see whether development in Sinuiju actually creates jobs and raises incomes. New facilities, roads, and housing are hard to count as a success if residents are hit with demands for money or forced labor mobilizations along the way. Beyond how the development looks, we need to see who bears the costs and who reaps the benefits.
articles.summary: 12 years after construction finished, the New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. Will North Korea's economy open too?

articles.title: A Warm Welcome for US Secretary of State in Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region.
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed the U.S. capital on October 17, bound for Uzbekistan and India, a journalist asked, “With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?” 
Rubio replied that it was the time that worked for the Central Asians. “This is an important relationship,” he added without expounding on that importance.
In response to questions from the Associated Press regarding Rubio’s schedule, the State Department said the secretary’s “responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight.”
The AP’s October 18 article was titled “Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he’s keeping the most pressing matters at a distance.” Rubio is involved in discussions on a blooming array of international crises, from Iran to China, Gaza to Ukraine, both in his role as secretary of state but also as national security adviser. But he’s not the public face of any of those issues, as the AP argued. 
“The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president’s broader national security objectives,” the State Department told the AP, pushing back against the implication that Rubio was avoiding tackling politically risky issues publicly. “The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue.”
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region. There is no free press in Samarkand lobbing difficult questions. There are no allies feeling sour about how much Washington has changed. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have been enthusiastic to endorse Trump administration initiatives, such as the Board of Peace, that traditional U.S. allies have avoided. 
In Samarkand, Rubio commented to the media that “Central Asia has simply not received the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now.” That’s a common refrain from the Trump administration, but it does not match reality. 
U.S. foreign policy regarding Central Asia over the last decade has been fairly consistent, as epitomized by the 11-year-old C5+1 format that brought Rubio to Samarkand in the first place to meet with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. 
The format was launched in 2015 when then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited all five regional countries in one trip – a feat Rubio promised to repeat last year during celebrations marking the C5+1’s 10th anniversary. While Rubio did meet bilaterally with the Central Asian foreign ministers, his only regional stop was in Uzbekistan. 
The overarching consistency of U.S. policy toward Central Asia does not mean nothing has changed. No longer do U.S. officials mention human rights or press freedom, areas which Central Asia’s autocratic governments score poorly on. And the Trump administration’s transactional style and its focus on business deals resonates with regional states, even as it narrows relations to the economic sphere. 
When Rubio’s trip to Uzbekistan was first announced in a late September press release from the U.S. Embassy in India – the U.S. ambassador to India is Sergio Gor, who also wears the hat of special envoy for South and Central Asian Affairs – it remarked that the secretary would be traveling with “a historic business delegation of more than 100 American companies.”
When the trip’s dates were announced in an October 13 press release, the delegation had become “over 200 business leaders.”
In Samarkand, Rubio referred to the commercial delegation as “incredible,” with representatives of almost 300 American businesses joining.
On October 14, The Diplomat had asked the State Department if it had a list of the participating businesses. That question went unanswered.
RFE/RL reported that the delegation would include representatives from Boeing, Citibank, and Franklin Templeton, “as well as businesses operating in critical minerals and other strategic sectors.”
In comments to RFE/RL, Daniel Rosenblum, formerly deputy assistant secretary of state for Central Asia from 2014 to 2019 and then U.S. ambassador to Uzbekistan (2019-2022) and Kazakhstan (2022-2025), noted that the secretary of state’s large business delegation was unusual but “may lead to more successes in terms of deals being signed and new investments.”
He added, however, that “the realities of investing in Central Asia remain the same.” He pointed to “the realities of distance, logistics, financing, finding a good partner. All of those things remain the same, regardless of whether you have 100 companies, 200 companies, or 20 companies.”
The joint statement published on October 19 – titled “C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future” – concluded with this: “We envision C5+1 cooperation that continues to deliver regional solutions to global challenges.” 
Of course, per usual with the Trump administration, those challenges don’t include climate change, a major complicating issue for regional states bent on building their future economies on the back of AI and mining, both of which are water and energy-intensive industries. And they didn’t touch on human rights, either. 
Instead, the statement highlighted trade and connectivity, specifically the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, as well as security. It references “untapped natural resources” and states, “we will combine our strengths to be a collective, powerful driver of regional energy sector development.”
As U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio departed the U.S. capital on October 17, bound for Uzbekistan and India, a journalist asked, “With everything going on in the world and with crisis all over, why are you choosing now, at this time, to go to Uzbekistan?” 
Rubio replied that it was the time that worked for the Central Asians. “This is an important relationship,” he added without expounding on that importance.
In response to questions from the Associated Press regarding Rubio’s schedule, the State Department said the secretary’s “responsibility is not to generate a public profile around every challenge; it is to help the president develop and execute a strategy that advances American interests. Some of the most consequential diplomatic work takes place outside the public spotlight.”
The AP’s October 18 article was titled “Rubio heads to Central Asia as some wonder if he’s keeping the most pressing matters at a distance.” Rubio is involved in discussions on a blooming array of international crises, from Iran to China, Gaza to Ukraine, both in his role as secretary of state but also as national security adviser. But he’s not the public face of any of those issues, as the AP argued. 
“The Iran, Gaza, and the Russia-Ukraine conflicts each demand serious attention, but they cannot be approached in isolation from the president’s broader national security objectives,” the State Department told the AP, pushing back against the implication that Rubio was avoiding tackling politically risky issues publicly. “The right question is not whether the secretary is visible enough on a particular issue.”
Not only can Rubio avoid the most pressing international crises by jetting off to Central Asia, but he – and the Trump administration more broadly – were guaranteed to receive a warm welcome in the region. There is no free press in Samarkand lobbing difficult questions. There are no allies feeling sour about how much Washington has changed. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have been enthusiastic to endorse Trump administration initiatives, such as the Board of Peace, that traditional U.S. allies have avoided. 
In Samarkand, Rubio commented to the media that “Central Asia has simply not received the level of attention from our policymakers over the last 20 years that it deserves. But that’s changing. That’s why we’re here now.” That’s a common refrain from the Trump administration, but it does not match reality. 
U.S. foreign policy regarding Central Asia over the last decade has been fairly consistent, as epitomized by the 11-year-old C5+1 format that brought Rubio to Samarkand in the first place to meet with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan. 
The format was launched in 2015 when then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited all five regional countries in one trip – a feat Rubio promised to repeat last year during celebrations marking the C5+1’s 10th anniversary. While Rubio did meet bilaterally with the Central Asian foreign ministers, his only regional stop was in Uzbekistan.

articles.title: South Korea, US Pull Apart as the Alliance Strains
articles.full_text:
Restricted intelligence sharing, an investment spat, and remarks by a U.S. commander point to a widening gap between the allies.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung meets with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York, Sep. 22, 2026.
South Korea and the United States are in a tug-of-war over the terms of their alliance. Since March the two governments have clashed over intelligence sharing, investment, and military command. The friction is now visible in small and concrete ways.
The dispute began on March 6 when the South’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young named the North Korean city of Kusong as the site of a uranium enrichment facility. Washington treated the remark as a disclosure of classified information and has since partially restricted the imagery intelligence shared with Seoul on North Korea. Chung has said he learned of the facility from open sources. Washington did not accept the explanation. In April, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac acknowledged that the two governments held different views of the remark.
A second dispute has become entangled with the first. The U.S.-listed e-commerce company Coupang is under investigation in South Korea over a data breach. A July report by the U.S. House Judiciary Committee accused South Korea’s National Intelligence Service of pressuring officials to pursue the company; the NIS called the claim false. In the same April briefing, Wi said the Coupang case concerned a single company. He nonetheless acknowledged that it was affecting security talks and delaying negotiations.
The intelligence service has been affected directly. Washington barred the agency from a June meeting with Japan on North Korean cyber threats and notified Seoul in writing, according to local media reports. The agency called the exclusion a one-time measure. South Korean Ambassador to the U.S. Kang Kyung-hwa also confirmed that visas for two or three agency employees bound for the embassy in Washington had been delayed. The agency attributed the delays to stricter U.S. entry procedures and denied any link to the intelligence dispute. 
Each incident can be explained on its own, but together the impact is mounting on the intelligence relationship. 
Economic pressure has followed a similar course. Seoul hoped that progress on its $350 billion investment pledge under a trade deal with Washington would restart stalled security talks on nuclear-powered submarines and uranium enrichment. However, the specific terms of investment have become a cause of more tension.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on September 30 that South Korea would invest $54 billion in the Alaska liquefied natural gas project. The trade ministry in Seoul said no decision had been made on whether to invest or how much. Trump pressed the point two days later. On October 2, he warned Seoul of higher costs for staying out of the project. He repeated the investment claim on October 14 in a post on Truth Social.
Before the November 3 midterm elections, Trump has been presenting investment pledges from allies as proof that his tariff policy works. Now Seoul is facing pressure to turn a campaign claim into a financial commitment. The link to security talks gives the dispute weight beyond money.
The strain is also jeopardizing a long-held South Korean military goal. The Lee administration aims to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces by 2028. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson – the officer who currently hold wartime OPCON over Korean forces – has cited the first quarter of 2029.
Then, on October 14, Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington that the conditions for the handover had changed. He pointed to recent North Korean missile launches as evidence. He voiced support for the OPCON transfer but opposed rushing it to meet a political deadline. 
South Korean Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said the next day that Seoul had already conveyed its concerns to Washington. The Defense Ministry maintained that the agreed conditions for the transfer remain unchanged.
On October 19, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung was asked about Brunson’s comments. Speaking at the presidential Blue House, Lee told reporters that Seoul must regain wartime OPCON quickly. He added that talks with Washington are basically moving toward its return. Lee also argued that the process should be called a recovery rather than a transfer. 
A second remark from Brunson drew sharper criticism in Seoul. The Demilitarized Zone is a buffer strip between the two Koreas, and the Military Demarcation Line runs through its middle. At the same forum, Brunson said that South Korea begins at the southern fence of the DMZ from the perspective of the United Nations Command. He commands the U.S.-led United Nations Command, which manages the zone to uphold the armistice. A command official countered that there was no question about South Korean sovereignty.
Lawmakers of the ruling Democratic Party objected. Kim Byung-joo, a special presidential adviser on defense policy, demanded a retraction and an apology. The constitution defines the territory of South Korea as the Korean Peninsula and its adjacent islands. Even read narrowly, the remark did little to reassure a partner seeking more control over its own defense.
This isn’t the first time Brunson had sparked controversy. In May, he had likened South Korea to a “dagger in the heart of Asia,” implying that the U.S. would use military assets stationed on the peninsula to thwart China’s “ambitions beyond that.” Seoul has conveyed its concerns about Brunson through several channels and reportedly received a sympathetic reply from the U.S. side.
The latest frictions in South Korea-U.S. relations came as North Korea stepped up its weapons tests. On October 15, North Korean state media reported that the country had tested two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles the day before. That followed a launch of tactical ballistic missiles on October 12. 
A land mine explosion wounded three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ on September 21. The South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff have determined that North Korea planted the mines.
On October 19, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement that South Korean troops had fired warning shots at North Korean personnel working on border fortifications. She accused South Korean forces of carrying out 2,870 loudspeaker warnings and 201 warning shots between August 1 and October 17. 
Kim added that the North Korean military was considering deploying more tactical strike weapons along the southern border and resuming loudspeaker broadcasts against the South. She also accused the Lee administration of escalating confrontation faster than his conservative predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol.
On one level, the alliance is still robust. Communication continues between South Korea and the U.S. as usual. But behind the facade of normal interactions, analysts worry that Seoul is increasingly facing steep costs for saying no to U.S. demands. Across intelligence, trade, and military command, Washington is interlinking issues so that Seoul faces restrictions and threats on all fronts. That looks more like a transactional relationship than the “ironclad” alliance the two foreign ministers reaffirmed on September 18. 
A partner that can only follow is not an ally in the full sense of the word.

articles.title: What the Greens Misunderstand About the Ukraine Conflict
articles.full_text:
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one. As a political position it is self-defeating, too.
At the end of September, the Australian Greens elected David Shoebridge their new leader. Shoebridge had previously been the party’s spokesperson for foreign affairs and defense, and he retained those responsibilities. While he has always been a combative politician, he immediately created controversy by stating it would be the Greens’ policy to oppose providing further military assistance to Ukraine. Extraordinarily, in a meeting with a number of Ukrainian-Australian community groups last week he left a further sour taste by informing them to not “burn any bridges” by criticizing the Greens.
Shoebridge has said that the party is one of “peace and non-violence,” but within this perspective comes a number of often naïve assumptions about international relations and how states manage conflict. It leads to an odd scenario whereby in proclaiming to be advocates of peace and nonviolence the Greens end up supporting belligerents over victims. 
There are some common traits that “pacifist” parties exhibit that are worth analyzing to understand the Greens’ position. 
The first is that they see violence as a self-perpetuating system. War creates a cycle of fear, militarization, and retaliation. The participants become trapped in an escalating security dilemma – each interpreting the other’s actions as a threat. Therefore peace requires breaking this cycle through restraint, negotiation, and disarmament. This may seem rational on the surface, but it doesn’t account for bad faith actors who believe solely in domination and cannot be trusted to honor any negotiated deal. This is the type of state Ukraine is facing with Russia. 
Alongside this, there is a distrust of the distinction between offensive and defensive power. There is a belief that all military power is essentially used for offensive purposes to varying degrees. Based on that assumption, states which arm themselves in defense – or become a part of an alliance system – are creating the conditions for aggressive actions to occur. Yet this assumes that larger states will naturally respect the sovereignty of their smaller neighbors if they are not armed. This, again, is a misunderstanding of Russia, which views weakness, not strength, as an incentive to escalate. 
What pacifists often believe is that nonviolent resistance is an underutilized alternative to military resistance. There have, of course, been instances where nonviolent resistance has proved incredibly effective, in India during British rule, for example. But nonviolent resistance relies on two factors – when an occupying force requires the assistance of the invaded population, and when this force has enough of a moral compass to be able form some empathy for those it has invaded. Russia simply does not believe that Ukraine is a legitimate nation-state. A disarmed Ukraine is a nonexistent Ukraine.
For some pacifists the priority is to stop conflict, even if the resulting settlement leaves the aggressor state with territorial or political gains. A ceasefire can be argued as saving lives. Yet any settlement that rewards aggression may be an encouragement for further aggression. Russia not only sees Ukraine as an illegitimate state, but also Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Georgia, and Moldova. Rewarding Russia for its invasion of Ukraine sends a signal that it can make military gains in these states too.  
The concept of deterrence is built on the assumption that there will always be belligerence in the world and that peace requires demonstrating and communicating clearly through credible military power that this belligerence will not succeed. For parties like the Greens this is a difficult assumption to swallow. Their belief is that peace can be secured through diplomacy and “good vibes” alone. 
The danger within this pacifism is that it becomes an inflexible political doctrine that treats a refusal to use force as a self-perceived moral victory, and overlooks the actual victims of violence. It confuses the insisted innocence of their own actions with the justice of a real world outcome. 
As a policy, the Greens decision to not support military assistance to Ukraine is a deeply flawed one, but as a political position it is self-defeating. Support for military assistance to Ukraine is a popular position in Australia, and many people believe that Australia should be doing more to help.
Support for the Greens themselves has plateaued at around 12 percent of the Australian public. The party’s approach is mostly to cultivate its status within this 12 percent and they seem disinclined to try to speak to anyone else. Therefore, the party’s position on military assistance to Ukraine probably has less to do with Ukraine itself, and was simply devised as a form of internal moral posturing with little comprehension how peace and security are actually achieved.

articles.title: Ecological Imbalance Is Driving Bear Encounters in Mongolia
articles.full_text:
As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns.
In recent months, Mongolia has experienced rare bear sightings in its northern provinces. Local authorities have so far been successful in capturing the bears alive and placing the animals back into their natural habitat. The sudden movement of such a large number of bears indicates a deeper ecological imbalance not only in Mongolia but also Russia and Japan. 
As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns. Solo bears, bears with cubs, and lost cubs have been sighted. More alarmingly, bears have encountered nomadic herders, killing one person and injuring several others. People from remote towns and herding communities have reported attacks on livestock. Most of these bears encounters have been reported in Khuvgsul, Bulgan, Darkhan-Uul, and Tuv provinces – all Mongolia’s northern provinces with robust habitat for bears, wolves, elk, deer, and wild boars.   
The sudden surge and the possible migration of bears clearly demonstrate the changing environment in their natural habitat. Khuvsgul, Bulgan, and Darkhan Uul provinces are 51 percent forest and considered a perfect habitat for bears. Mongolia’s boreal forests, known as taiga, offer cedar and pine nuts, types of berries, and water access for bears. In the fall, particularly in the months of August, September, and October, bears forage throughout the taiga with their cubs in preparation for hibernation. 
The increased movement of these bear populations points to several issues in Mongolia’s ecological system. One of the speculated causes is a shortage of food. Mongolia’s extreme weather fluctuations, including shorter summers with amplified heatwaves, can impact vegetation and dry out grasslands. Particularly in Khuvsgul and Bulgan, given the short summer, there is a risk of shortage of berries and nuts. 
In addition, Khuvsgul and Selenge provinces hold one of Mongolia’s critical river basins, which is crucial to the forestry and its natural habitat. One of the remaining questions concerning bear movements is whether these river basins and other water sources are experiencing a fish shortage, caused by climate change and mining activities. 
Given the pristine nature of Northern Mongolia, these provinces are subject to strict environmental scrutiny and protection. Still, mining does occur. Bulgan Province, in particular, is known for its extractive industries, including gold and polymetallic mining (although in comparison to other notable extractive sites, the scale of mining in Bulgan is relatively moderate). 
According to the World Resources Institute, Mongolia’s gold rush has become one of the leading sources of water contamination. Gold extraction sites particularly are a major issue for the local environment. “Lead, arsenic and other toxic chemicals released during gold extraction processes have leached into Mongolia’s groundwater and flowed untreated into rivers,” the WRI found. 
Thus Mongolia’s bear sightings may be related to the country’s mining activities, along with extreme weather aggravated by climate change-caused food shortages. In response, the government and conservation groups are taking a humane approach. Local authorities and the population continue to capture bears and place them back into the wild. 
In comparison, Russia and Japan, both experiencing a similar bear issue, are handling it very differently.   
In Russia’s Far East, in the Siberian forests, the bear population thrives. This October, local authorities in Siberia (Krasnoyarsk), Tuva, and Buryatia reported a surge of bears entering local towns and villages. In Buryatia, the local authority has deployed 24 specialized teams to kill bears. With Russian authorities allowing an “open season,” bear killings will likely increase. 
In 2025, the Environmental Ministry of Japan reported a historic surge in bear sightings and attacks, during which more than 14,600 bears were killed. The ministry believed that “climate change and poor tree-nut harvests have reduced natural food supplies in the mountains.” The ministry also highlighted that around 12,000 brown bears in Hokkaido and Asiatic black bears elsewhere have expanded their roaming range. 
While Northeast Asia faces a shared ecological challenge in conserving bear populations and managing their movements, Mongolia, Russia, and Japan have adopted vastly different approaches. Mongolia emphasizes strict legal protections and non-lethal management whereas Russia and Japan both have implemented aggressive population control methods. 
According to Rebecca Watters, founder and director of the Mongolian Wolverine Project and a biologist, bears are attracted to any kind of predictable food source. Once they associate people with food – in the form of garbage, livestock, gardens, birdfeeders, etc. – they will continue to seek out human settlements. 
In Mongolia’s case specifically, she added, “I wonder too whether some of the increase in sightings and conflict is due to population shifts, in both people and the bears. Paradoxically, some of these issues might also be related to conservation successes and more bears cubs surviving.”
