The sudden movement of such a large number of bears indicates a deeper ecological imbalance not only in Mongolia but also Russia and Japan.
articles.summary: As of early October, the Mongolian authorities have received 754 calls reporting bear sightings in various provinces and towns.

articles.title: What Is Behind Bangladesh’s Continuing Law and Order Crisis?
articles.full_text:
The government must rebuild public trust in the police force and insulate law enforcement from political influence.
On October 12, Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), a Bangladeshi rights organization, reported that between July and September this year, 17 people were killed and 1,227 injured in 183 incidents of political violence in Bangladesh. This was a 12 percent increase in the number of incidents in the same period last year. Mob violence also rose sharply from 98 to 137.
These figures indicate that the Bangladeshi state is struggling to stabilize and normalize the law and order situation in the country since the revolutionary mobilization in 2024. So, the transition from the previous authoritarian ecosystem under Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League to the new democratic ecosystem has faced several challenges.
According to data from the human rights organization, Ain o Salish Kendra, deaths from mob violence increased from 51 in 2023 to 128 in 2024 and 197 in 2025. Police say that registered murder cases increased from 3,023 in 2023 to 3,786 in 2025. Besides that, reports of incidents of extortion, political clashes, and armed violence have raised concerns about the deteriorating law and order situation in Bangladesh.
After the fall of Hasina’s authoritarian regime in August 2024, public ire was directed against law and enforcement authorities; 450 of Bangladesh’s 639 police stations became nonfunctional following attacks, while approximately 30 percent of police positions were left temporarily vacant.
Building trust in the police forces was a daunting task. There was little trust in the police force to begin with, thanks to the colonial policing culture that East Pakistan and then Bangladesh inherited, and even embraced. Successive regimes initially used the police as a tool not so much to enforce law and order as to stifle dissent. Political connections and corruption determined professional advancement within the police force. As a result, the Bangladesh police were hardly a professional force.
Ahead of the 2024 national election, nearly 10,000 opposition activists were arrested, while politically motivated cases, enforced disappearances, and extrajudicial killings became recurring instruments of repression. Police authorities were reportedly involved in almost 708 enforced disappearance cases. Some also threatened women with rape if they didn’t fall in line.
The Hasina regime used the police to weaken its opponents, and as many officers became tools of the regime, the ladder to climb the ranks was less about hard work than about loyalty to the government and serving its agenda. For example, 349 police officers received awards, including one who received recognition for arresting photographer Shahidul Alam over his criticism of the government.
This broken and untrustworthy ecosystem could not be fixed in a few days, weeks or even months. When the anti-Hasina protests ended, people guarded the streets as the whole police and law-and-order maintenance system broke apart.
Even routine policing has become a challenge in Bangladesh. Officers who previously operated with strong political backing now face considerable risks when intervening in confrontations. Although the interim regime intervened to restore the law and order mechanism and revive the working of police stations, it has been difficult for people to trust the police.
The color of police uniforms and the logo of the police force were changed twice, but these superficial adjustments had little impact on how the public perceived the police.
Then came initiatives to rebuild the police force. However, a member of the Police Reform Commission that was set up post-2024 told The Diplomat that the recommendations for reforming the police have not been taken seriously by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government. It has not taken a single step towards reforming the police force, he said. As a result, public perception of the police force has not improved much. According to a survey by the International Republican Institute, 52 percent of respondents disapproved of the police’s performance, while 45 percent approved. Of all of Bangladesh’s public institutions surveyed, the police force secured the lowest public approval
Another reason for the poor law and order situation in Bangladesh is the changing structure of political authority at the grassroots level. During the Awami League’s 15 years in power, local political and economic influence was largely concentrated within very systematized networks connected to the ruling party. Control over transport terminals, markets, construction contracts, land, and other economic resources was often exercised through internally negotiated and mutually established political patronage networks. So the division and the hierarchy were clear.
The fall of the Awami League disrupted this hierarchy. Individuals and groups previously excluded from local power structures began competing for positions and resources formerly controlled by these networks. The clash for the new owner of the throne was on the table, and local political competition became intertwined with disputes over extortion, property, markets, and territorial influence. In May alone, Dhaka Metropolitan Police identified 1,280 active extortionists in the capital, including 148 armed criminals. Throughout the country, 600 incidents of political violence were documented between August 2024 and December 2025, resulting in 158 deaths and more than 7,000 injuries, where many confrontations involved struggles over local dominance and economic resources.
These rivalries have continued after the BNP formed the government in February this year. Of the 183 political-violence incidents documented by HRSS between July and September this year, 69 involved internal BNP conflicts, while another 92 involved confrontations between BNP members and other political groups.  Rival factions seeking influence within the same political organization have become an important source of conflict and violence at the grassroots level.
So, post-2024, Bangladesh has entered an endless loop of conflicts as rival political groups compete for local authority. The government seems unable to control the police, even as the latter are weak and lack the moral authority to solve the problem. And most significantly, in this process, conflicts are reinforcing each other.
It is time that the BNP government wakes up to the grave law and order situation in the country. Its immediate task should be to rebuild police authority without restoring political control over policing.
The Police Commission Ordinance adopted in December 2025, which was intended to strengthen oversight and accountability, has since ceased to have effect. This means that the legal framework designed to regulate police conduct is no longer operative, leaving oversight mechanisms unenforced. Without institutional independence, the police risk becoming dependent on political patronage again, while competition over local resources continues to encourage violence.
Establishing law and order in Bangladesh will need more than increasing police deployment or arresting individual criminals. Otherwise, the country risks replacing one system of politically controlled order with another, without establishing the rule of law that the July uprising promised.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Counterterrorism Campaign Is at an Inflection Point
articles.full_text:
If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the causes.
Pakistan security forces search a car in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa for weapons, Oct. 18, 2026.
For the last several years, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) has been the epicenter of terrorism in Pakistan. However, 2026 marks an exception to this rule, as Balochistan has emerged as the most volatile region in terms of both the number of attacks and casualties. As of October 19, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal’s open-source data, Balochistan had suffered 1,147 terrorist attacks, and 2,394 deaths (424 civilians, 736 security personnel, and 1,233 insurgents or terrorists, plus one death that was not categorized). However, numbers provide only one aspect of a disturbing and complex security situation.
With 12 of KP’s 36 districts witnessing a worsening law-and-order situation and a receding writ of the state, Pakistan recently imposed emergency and governor’s rule in the province. Two militant networks, Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP), have been carrying out large-scale attacks from their hideouts in Afghanistan and reconstituted networks in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border areas. Since the Taliban’s return to power, the organizational coherence, operational capacity, recruitment strategies, propaganda methods, and fundraising techniques of these terrorist networks have significantly evolved.
Against this backdrop, Pakistan’s counterterrorism approach must be grounded in an accurate assessment of a complex and fluid threat landscape. Taking an over-simplistic view of a complicated threat picture would result in temporary respite instead of permanent peace. Therefore, taking a holistic and nuanced view of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s security situation is the first step in restoring peace in the province.
Terrorism in KP predates the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s (PTI) three successive governments in the province. In fact, its contemporary roots can be traced to the May 1994 Malakand uprising of Sufi Muhammad’s Tehreek-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Muhammadi (TNSM). Since then, terrorism has persisted in KP in one form or another. Therefore, terrorism in the province is despite, and not because of, the PTI’s provincial regime. The PTI’s lack of cooperation is just one of the several factors that have contributed to a worsening law-and-order situation in the restive province. Nevertheless, it is quite unfortunate that the PTI politicized internal security.
Pakistan’s flawed pro-Taliban Afghan policy, kinetic-heavy counterterrorism approach, governance deficit, underdeveloped non-kinetic counterterrorism framework (or a Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism policy), and absence of structural reforms have cumulatively contributed to the current security situation in KP. If the new security framework fails to adopt a holistic approach to counterterrorism, it will once again end up treating the symptoms while ignoring the root causes.
Since the military is Pakistan’s most developed and capable security institution, the country has heavily leaned on it to suppress terrorism. By and large, military operations have proved successful in dismantling terrorist networks, their command-and-control nodes, organizational infrastructure, and logistical pipelines. However, the absence of political processes required to translate those tactical advantages into permanent strategic gains reversed improvements in security.
Going forward, transparent and timely strategic communication is crucial in fighting and discrediting terrorist networks. Pakistani security institutions must ensure transparent and timely communication grounded in the rule-of-law approach to reclaim the narrative domain from violent nonstate actors. They must provide a realistic assessment to the public that the military has no magic wand to bring an overnight improvement in the security situation. It will be a long struggle before peace can be restored. The first step would be to reduce the intensity of terrorist attacks and their impact. Then, large-scale kinetic operations will be required to blunt the sharp edge of terrorism.
Here, strategic communication is important. It will involve a two-pronged effort. First, the government must comprehensively address public concerns about why previous operations, despite their mixed results, were necessary. Faulting them alone for terrorism’s recurrence is unfair. The blame equally goes to the absence of political processes and good governance. There is a need for constitutional and administrative reforms too.
Second, the government must unambiguously convey to the masses how and why the new counterterrorism operations will be different from their previous iterations. Persistent and timely communication to the public will bridge the existing perception gaps about previous counterterrorism policies and their outcomes. Especially in the age of social media, terrorists are exploiting communication gaps and information blackouts. Malevolent actors jump into these situations to misguide public perception through misinformation and disinformation campaigns. Therefore, ensuring continuous and consistent communication about the progress of counter-terrorism operations and challenges confronting them will be critical.
Likewise, unlike in the past, the security institutions will do well to avoid premature victory declarations.  Such pronouncements, especially without consolidating security gains through kinetic operations into permanent strategic advantages, can result in complacency and a false sense of security. This time around, the absence of violence must not be mistaken for peace. This happened during the 2015-2020 period when a decline in terrorist attacks and the displacement of terrorist networks was confused with their elimination. The premature victory trap is tempting but dangerous, as it erodes public trust, which is central to the success of counterterrorism initiatives.
Similarly, a clear distinction between eliminating terrorists and terrorism is important. Terrorists, despite their elimination, keep returning to the battlefield as long as the roots of terrorism are not adequately tackled. Terrorism keeps the recruitment pipeline alive by exploiting ideological, political, and socioeconomic grievances. Terrorism is effectively tackled when terrorists are ideologically and discursively discredited to a point where the masses reject their appeal despite having reservations about the state. For that, strengthening state-society relations, or renewing the social contract, is important. The glue that keeps states and societies together is governance. Making state policies and administrative apparatus receptive to people’s needs and demands will drain the swamp where terrorists germinate.
Finally, terrorism in Pakistan has its internal and external dimensions. Internal consolidation against terrorist networks constitutes a necessary but not sufficient condition to overcome the challenge of terrorism. Pakistan will have to evolve a two-pronged policy, involving proactive diplomacy and coercion.
Diplomatically, Pakistan must highlight the Taliban’s support for the TTP, IMP, and Baloch separatist groups. At the same time, Pakistan should impose punitive costs on Kabul for allowing Afghanistan’s soil to be used for cross-border terrorism against it. Pakistani air strikes in Afghanistan should aim to destroy terrorist hideouts as well as the Taliban’s military capabilities to a point where they revisit their strategic calculus of supporting the TTP and IMP.
The declaration of emergency in KP marks an inflection point in the evolution of Pakistan’s counterterrorism policy. A prudent, holistic, transparent, and proactive approach with a long-term vision will deliver peace dividends. A reactive, kinetic-heavy approach, lacking concomitant non-kinetic interventions and a transparent communication strategy, will deliver short-term respite at the cost of long-term peace.

articles.title: After War of Words, China Says Relations With Philippines at ‘Critical Juncture’
articles.full_text:
Growing political polarization has the potential to undermine Manila’s ability to handle its ongoing maritime disputes with Beijing.
China on Friday expressed willingness to improve its relationship with the Philippines, but admitted that relations were at “an extremely sensitive and critical juncture” due to the actions of unnamed “outside forces.”
The two governments have been engaged in a war of words since Friday, when Jing Quan, China’s ambassador to Manila, declared that China could “easily win” a war with the Philippines. Jing was responding to a remark by Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro, who the day prior described China as the lone “troublemaker” in Southeast Asia, due to its aggressive actions in contested parts of the South China Sea.
Speaking to the press after a Diliman Dialogues organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City, Jing said that the remark was “nonsense.”
“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region,” he said. “If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force, and we love peace. In this region, we enjoy peace.”
Asked on Friday about Ambassador Jing’s remark, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr ‌said that ⁠it “sounds very much like a threat” and that he would summon the ambassador to provide an explanation. Jing, who began his posting last December, was previously summoned by Marcos in July, after a Philippine marine was injured in a melee with the China Coast Guard at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands and the subsequent publication of a video by the state-run China Daily depicting Filipinos as monkeys and U.S. puppets.
Yesterday, the Chinese embassy issued a statement in which it said it considered the Philippines a “close neighbor and friend with deep historical and cultural ties.” It also said the Philippines need not choose between China and the United States and that the two sides “should maintain dialogue, manage differences, and expand cooperation in trade, investment, people-to-people exchanges, and law enforcement.”
At the same time, it said that China-Philippines relations were “at an extremely sensitive and critical juncture and require prudent, careful handling” and lambasted “anti-China politicians” who it said, “deliberately ignore China’s clear and consistent position on China-Philippines relations, instead twisting its words out of context and maliciously distorting the facts for political gain.”
It concluded by saying that differences “should be managed through dialogue” and that “outside forces” – i.e., the United States and its allies – “should not be allowed to steer bilateral relations toward confrontation.”
“China is ready to work with all sectors of Philippine society to promote dialogue, deepen trust, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation,” it added.
Such exchanges have taken place periodically between the two governments over the past few years, often linked to events in the South China Sea, where the two nations have overlapping maritime claims. Besides, Chinese and Philippine coast guards have engaged in a string of confrontations, some involving the use of physical force, which have pushed relations to their worst point in years.
Jing’s comments were preceded by a chain of public comments and responses emanating from the Philippines’ fractious domestic politics, hinting at the apparent growing polarization of foreign relations along partisan lines.
This began on October 6 with the airing of allegations that Chinese entities had sent just over $5 million in remittances to a Philippine company linked to the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, a major rival of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. The claims, which came to light during Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in the Senate, prompted Marcos to state that the involvement of Chinese money made the issue “a national security issue.”
“If it is true, it is a threat – a threat at the highest level to the republic,” Marcos said on October 12.
Duterte responded the same day by stating that the Philippines was becoming the main “troublemaker of Southeast Asia” by treating business ties with China as a national security concern. Teodoro’s comment about China being the main “troublemaker” in the region was a direct response to Duterte. At this point, Jing made his incautious entry into the “debate,” turning the domestic war of words into a potential diplomatic incident.
The incident is notable for what it says about how bitter political rivalries in the Philippines have the potential to impact Manila’s delicate balancing of relations with China and the United States. In late 2016, the administration of President Rodrigo Duterte, Sara’s father, initiated a bold turn toward China, downplaying maritime disputes in order to gain Chinese financial support for major infrastructure projects. The needle swung back under Marcos, who, after coming to office in 2022, strengthened the Philippines’ relationship with the United States and became much more forceful in his condemnations of Chinese behavior in the South China Sea.
There is now some danger that as the country moves toward the next presidential election in 2028, the two rival camps will come to see benefits in depicting each other as agents of foreign forces (the U.S. and China, respectively). The impacts of this could stretch beyond the periodic diplomatic incident. Indeed, they could begin to impact Manila’s ability to maintain a stable and predictable approach toward the challenges posed by China’s aggressive actions in the South China Sea.

articles.title: Deepavali vs Diwali Sparks New Political Row in Malaysia
articles.full_text:
Is the Malaysian Indian Congress using Hindu identity politics to regain its political relevance ahead of the next general election?
Deepavali rangoli artwork at Berjaya Times Square, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Nov. 11, 2012.
In India, religious sentiment has become such a fragile commodity that it can be hurt by almost anything: a joke, a film song, a movie title, or even a slogan printed on a T-shirt.
Far from India, a slight change in spelling and pronunciation has sparked a political maelstrom. In Malaysia, the Hindu festival of lights is celebrated as a public holiday. This time a controversy erupted because the traditional terminology, “Deepavali,” was not used in public greetings.
After Kuala Lumpur City Hall erected festive arches wishing the public a “Happy Diwali,” M. Saravanan, deputy president of the Malaysian Indian Congress (MIC), accused the authorities of erasing the traditional terminology. For him, the change in spelling has become a question of cultural identity and religious sentiment.
Saravanan subsequently wrote to Hannah Yeoh, minister in the Prime Minister’s Department responsible for Federal Territories, asking her to restore the legally gazetted name. He said that the choice of name was not merely a matter of semantics but one of respect for the linguistic and cultural heritage of Malaysian Hindus.

articles.title: Indonesian Stock Exchange Plunges After Fresh MSCI Downgrade Threat
articles.full_text:
Citing the lack of action on promised reforms, the global index provider has proposed demoting the country from “emerging market” to “standalone market” status.
The corporate headquarters of the Indonesia Stock Exchange in Jakarta, Indonesia, Jan. 23, 2025.
Indonesia’s stock market fell more than 11 percent on Friday, the steepest one-day drop since 1998, after the global index provider MSCI proposed the country’s removal ‌from its global stock indexes.
In a statement on Friday, MSCI said that it had launched “a consultation on a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes from Emerging Market to Standalone Market status.”
The proposal is more serious than MSCI’s earlier threat, announced in January to downgrade Indonesia from “emerging market” to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market. Chief among these were the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares – i.e., those openly available for public trading.
On Friday, MSCI again cited “significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market, including persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behavior.”
MSCI said it would procure feedback from market participants until the end of April 2027, and then announce its decision by June 30.
MSCI’s role as the primary benchmark for institutional investors gives it considerable power over emerging economies. As Reuters explains, a downgrade to “standalone” status “would exclude Indonesian stocks from indexes tracked by global funds, potentially triggering billions of dollars in capital outflows.”
Markets responded to the news as one would expect, with the Jakarta Composite Index falling by 11.6 percent, losing $65 of value. It was the largest single-day drop since the Asian financial crisis.
After MSCI’s January announcement, which also caused a hemorrhage in Indonesian equity markets, Indonesia announced a long list of reforms to address MSCI’s concerns, including a doubling of the ​minimum free float for listed companies to 15 percent. Top executives of the exchange and regulatory body also ​stepped down.
However, in its statement on Friday, MSCI said that “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market.”
“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement,” it stated. “Feedback from market participants suggests that a reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognize the depth of the market problems.”
MSCI said that it “expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification” barring clear evidence of “material improvements in market governance and functioning.”
If downgraded, Indonesia would join Argentina, Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Zimbabwe in the standalone category, becoming both the largest economy and the only Asia-Pacific market in the grouping. MSCI has said that reclassification to “standalone” status is typically done in cases of “severe deterioration in market accessibility or size and liquidity.”
The announcement, which came ahead of MSCI’s expected verdict on Indonesia’s reclassification to “frontier” status next month, came as a shock to many observers. Rully Arya Wisnubroto, head of research at Mirae Asset Sekuritas in Jakarta, told Reuters that the proposal “goes well beyond what we had considered our worst-case scenario.” Another analyst described it as “a wake-up call for Indonesia.”
Reza Priyambada, an analyst and director at Reliance Sekuritas, told the Jakarta Globe that given the reputational impact a downgrade to “standalone” status would have, the government had to act urgently to show it was serious about reform.
“Reforms should not focus solely on market development and the enforcement of sanctions,” he told the paper. “Authorities also need to ensure a level playing field in market mechanisms and address other issues that shape international investors’ assessments of the quality of Indonesia’s capital market.”
If the government fails to stave off a downgrade, it would severely impact Indonesia’s attractiveness as a destination for foreign investment and put significant pressure on President Prabowo Subianto, whose administration has marked a break with the conservative financial stewardship of its predecessors.
Coming to office in late 2024, the former general set an ambitious goal of 8 percent annual GDP growth for the rest of his term, and has introduced a number of high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, that, along with the global spike in fuel prices, have widened the fiscal deficit. Prabowo has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s returns from natural resources and international trade.
The president’s pugnacious and highly personalized style of governance, which has affected everything from fiscal policy to foreign relations, is at the root of much investor concern. In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for the country, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.”
Perceptions have also been shaped by the growing sense of volatility and unpredictability in how Indonesian institutions as a whole operate. A good example is the jailing in June of Gojek co-founder Nadiem Makarim, previously a leading member of Indonesia’s tech scene, on flimsy corruption charges related to the procurement of Google Chromebooks during his time as education minister.
As one observer noted at the time, the Nadiem case confirmed many investors’ perception of Indonesia as a country where “the line between a business decision, a policy misjudgment, and a prosecutable offense is drawn after the fact by whoever holds power at the time.”
As a reflection of the general economic malaise, the rupiah has fallen to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June.
In addition to the aforementioned reforms, the Prabowo administration has reshuffled its economic team in a bid to restore investor confidence. In July, the governor of the central bank stepped down, followed by Prabowo’s replacement of his finance minister in September. It will no doubt also announce a host of new reforms in the days and weeks to come.
Whether all of this has much effect on MSCI’s verdict remains to be seen. Judging by the wording of its latest announcement, some kind of downgrade for Indonesia is certain; it is now merely a question of how severe the shock will be.

articles.title: Exercise Tarang Shakti: A Mirror to India’s Multipronged Engagements
articles.full_text:
The exercise reflects two trends: the Indian military’s deepening interoperability with key partner nations, and India’s multi-vector foreign policy.
An Indian Air Force HAL Tejas leads a formation of a Mikoyan MiG-29UPG, Dassault Mirage 2000, Dassault Rafale, SEPECAT Jaguar, and Sukhoi Su-30MKI during Tarang Shakti 26 over Jodhpur, India, Oct. 2, 2026.
“The defense relationships of the future will be about technology and trust, not just about platforms,” India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said at an event and demonstration in Jodhpur on October 10 as the multilateral Exercise Tarang Shakti neared its end. A fly-past after that featured an arrow-shaped formation that included the Indian Air Force Su-30MKI (Russian origin) at the center, flanked on one side by a U.S. F-35 and an Indian Light Combat Aircraft (LCA), and on the other side by a French Rafale and an F-16 of the United Arab Emirates Air Force. This was an impressive formation; the technology and firepower they represented cannot be easily beaten.
An American fifth-generation fighter flying alongside a Russian-origin jet bears testimony to India’s multi-pronged foreign policy and military engagements.
Beyond Tarang Shakti, some bilateral exercises have culminated while others are lined up, showcasing the busy calendar of India’s military diplomacy and military-to-military engagements. For instance, at Vladivostok in Russia, the Indian and Russian Navies are holding their annual Indra exercise from October 13 to 18.
Together, these reflect two trends: one is the Indian military’s deepening interoperability across land, sea and air with key partner nations and like-minded countries, and the other is India’s multi-vectored foreign policy in line with its much-espoused strategic autonomy.
A biennial exercise, Tarang Shakti is now in its second edition.  It was themed “Power in Partnership” and was held at Jodhpur near India’s western borders. It commenced on September 26 and ended on October 12.  It brought together the Indian Air Force (IAF) and seven other countries – Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the UAE, and the U.S. – who deployed their aerial assets. Thirty-two other nations participated as observers.
The real metric of an exercise’s utility is not what the host nation deploys but what partner nations bring in, reflective of the value they see from it. The U.S. fifth-generation F-35 jets exercised over Indian skies for the first time, operating alongside the entire gamut of IAF fighters – the LCA, Rafale, SU-30MKI, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars, French Rafales and the UAE’s F-16s. These were completed by A-400M and C-130/ C-130J transport aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, G-6000 and other support platforms. An IAF official, citing a post-exercise data brief, told The Diplomat that Tarang Shakti saw more than 800 sorties and 600 hours flown.
The U.S. Pacific Air Forces deployed six F-35A Lightning IIs and one KC-135R Stratotanker along with over 200 personnel. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, U.S. Ambassador in India Sergio Gor remarked that their F-35s do not go all over the world and termed their presence at Tarang Shakti as “another example of trust” between the two countries. France, a resident Indian Ocean power, fielded four Rafales, three A330 Phoenix aerial refuellers, two A400M transport aircraft and 300 personnel. This was part of its larger Pegase26 mission that set out on September 8, traveling across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific, Middle East and North Africa. Over 40 days across nine destinations and covering over 40,000 miles, the mission demonstrates its capacity for long-range deployment, sustenance and adaptability.
Exercises typically involve subject matter exchanges, and India, as the host nation, utilized this to brief visitors on the outcomes of Operation Sindoor of May 2025, which has generated significant operational lessons for military planners. Encapsulating this, Exercise Director Air Vice Marshal Raj Thakur noted that Operation Sindoor was one of the remarkable operations carried out by India, and there was a lot of interest in knowing about it. “And that’s why in one of the subject matter expert exchanges, we briefed them about what exactly has happened in Operation Sindoor and our part of the story, and that was very well received,” Thakur said.
India has had a very busy diplo-military calendar in recent years. These were quite often simultaneous engagements with nations that are warring or adversaries. To appreciate the busy calendar and the diversity of engagements by the Indian military, it is worth looking at some of the notable engagements since July.
The India-U.S. bilateral Army exercise Yudh Abhyas was conducted from September 15 to 27. It saw 600 personnel from each side exercise at a high-altitude area at Auli in Uttarakhand, followed by long-range firepower drills, including U.S. HIMARS, Indian Pinaka rocket systems, and counter-drone systems in action, at Mahajan Field Firing Range in Rajasthan. Yudh Abhyas began in 2004 as a platoon-level exercise focused on peacekeeping operations and has since significantly expanded in scope and complexity. This is the case with all other India-U.S. military exercises: Cope India, the bilateral air exercise, or Exercise Malabar, which began as a bilateral naval exercise, have now become quadrilateral exercises featuring submarines and aircraft carriers practicing highly complex scenarios.
In addition to Yudh Abhyas, the Indian Army held bilateral wargames with Thailand (Maitree-XV), Mongolia (Nomadic Elephant), Kazakhstan (KAZIND) and UAE (Mountain Guardian), whether incoming or outgoing, with the last one set to conclude on October 18.
The Indian Navy has been the busiest with at least eight engagements. In addition to Indra, a trilateral exercise between India, Brazil and South Africa (Exercise IBSAMAR) is currently underway off South Africa. The Quad grouping, which includes India, Australia, Japan and the U.S., conducted a Tabletop Exercise on September 3 and 4 hosted by Japan to advance the Quad Indo-Pacific Logistics Network. In end-September, Quad Coast Guards carried out the second joint sail under the QUAD‑at‑Sea Ship Observer Mission. Indian Coast Guard Ship Shaunak sailed from Chennai on September 25 for Perth in Australia with six sea riders—two officers each from India and Japan, and one officer each from Australia and the U.S. embarked.
On October 8, the Indian Coast Guard conducted the 12th national Maritime Search and Rescue Exercise (SAREX-2026) off the coast of Odisha, which in addition to all Indian stakeholders, had 32 observers from 30 countries. It underscores the extent of deepening engagement, especially in the maritime domain, which has implications far and wide.
The IAF held two bilateral exercises with Japan (Veer Guardian) and Malaysia (Udara Shakti). More importantly, it joined the multilateral exercise Pitch Black hosted by the Royal Australian Air Force from July 7 to August 7.
The oft-repeated “interoperability” is more than just flying together in a fly past. It is extremely complex, necessitating understanding tactics, techniques, procedures, and cultural practices to seamlessly integrate the diverse range of equipment while also preserving one’s sensitive operational aspects. For instance, while the U.S. F-35s took part in war games, they were kept away from any prying eyes, even of the participating nations, highlighting the sensitivity of its most advanced technology. This prompted Air  Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh to take a friendly jibe at Gen. Kevin Schneider, the U.S. Pacific Air Forces Commander. At a press conference on October 10, the IAF chief pointed out: “Your people don’t even let us go near the aircraft, and you talk about selling it to us.”
While deepening engagements point to the evolving balancing and hedging in the Indo-Pacific, exercises are a way to prepare for evolving threats rather than be directed at anyone. This was underscored by Air Chief Singh at a press conference along with other chiefs and heads of participating forces. As far as the Indo-Pacific is concerned, the exercise was not meant to be projecting anything in any region, Singh stressed.
What do these exercises translate to in real time? As Gen. Schneider succinctly put it, “We don’t know what the security situation holds or what the future holds. Some of us may be called to do humanitarian assistance disaster relief, or there may be other challenges that we face. But when we come together, we don’t do it cold; we do it on a foundation of teamwork that is established at Tarang Shakti, Pitch Black, Red Flag Alaska, or the myriad of other exercises that take place throughout the Indo-Pacific region.”
Both Exercise Tarang Shakti and Exercise Yudh Abhyas were barometers of the extent of interoperability that has been achieved over the years by India with its key strategic partners.
The aim of Tarang Shakti was to enhance mutual understanding of tactical air power application, strengthen interoperability among participating Air Forces, and foster seamless multinational cooperation through integrated air operations, joint administration, logistics support, and maintenance coordination, a handout given at the event said. From the feedback and observations of participants, the exercise seems to have achieved what it set out to do.
It only reiterates India’s continuing expansion of military-to-military engagements in various formats and across geographies in line with its strategic objectives and in turn, the outcomes shaping the objectives.

articles.title: Cambodia’s NGO Sector Is Collapsing. Does It Matter?
articles.full_text:
Imported by international donors in the 1990s, NGOs have supplanted rather than strengthened local forms of political organizing.
A dusty road in Treak village, Siem Reap province, Cambodia.
From the early 1990s through the early 2010s, Cambodia hosted one of the most vibrant, generously funded, and unchecked civil society ecosystems in Southeast Asia. Former Prime Minister Hun Sen once famously referred to the country as a “heaven for NGOs.” And indeed, up to 6,100 registered non-government organizations (NGOs) and associations have been able to flourish, including about 3,450 NGOs and 2,650 other civil society associations. This number of NGOs is very high by global standards, by one count making up the second highest number per capita in the world after Rwanda.
A confluence of disasters has changed all that. The heyday for NGOs effectively started closing following the 2013 national elections, when the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) faced a major electoral threat and began systematically dismantling the public sphere. Viewing NGOs as a vehicle for hostile foreign-backed “color revolutions,” the Cambodian government introduced a restrictive and controversial Law on Associations and Non-Governmental Organizations in 2015. It also began to use tax audits, lawsuits, and political pressure – such as monitoring or disturbing civil society meetings, refusing to give permission for activities, and other coercive tactics – to restrict the sector.
Not only are NGOs required to navigate a suspicious and unfriendly political environment, but they also face a critically strained financial environment. Recently, the international development landscape has endured its steepest funding decline on record. As global power relations go through a process of significant reconfiguration and Cambodia simultaneously moves toward graduating from Least Developed Country status in 2029, global official development aid has been dramatically curtailed. This is set to continue.
The dramatic reduction in funds has had a significant and increasing impact on Cambodia and its NGOs. Already 10 years have passed since funding for Cambodian NGOs reached its peak in 2016. A recent survey of civil society organizations in Cambodia revealed that 26 percent of NGOs say they are not financially viable beyond 2027. It is not unreasonable to suggest that only one in five NGOs may survive the next decade.
In response to this calamity, there have been calls to redesign the ecosystem of civil society in Cambodia. These are led by the Cooperation Committee of Cambodia (CCC), which serves as the professional association of NGOs. A roadmap prepared by the CCC points to how major transformation can be achieved. Options being considered include increased reliance on local philanthropy; the reinvention of NGOs as social enterprises or technical assistance offices; blended financing; increased sharing of resources and organizational infrastructure; and, if there is interest, mergers.
If undertaken, these initiatives would together mark a profound shift away from traditional NGO models toward leaner, more specialized structures grounded in local ownership.
First, local philanthropy is captured almost exclusively by the CPP and, for the purposes of making merit, by pagodas and other institutions associated with Buddhist practice. There is little appetite among everyday citizens for giving to NGOs, and it seems unreasonable to expect NGOs to try and compete with entrenched political parties and organized religion in their fundraising efforts. A notable exception to NGOs’ failure to inspire local giving is the Cambodian Red Cross, which is skilled at generating significant donations from wealthy individuals. While this is a large and prominent humanitarian organization in Cambodia specializing in disaster relief, it is also compromised by political entanglements – its president is Hun Sen’s wife Bun Rany – and is the recipient of questionable major donations.
In any event, international philanthropy sometimes funds the wrong things, as any effective altruist will tell you. Well-meaning donors tend to give to projects that look good or feel good, not necessarily those that do good. Just this week, Sunrise Cambodia, a Cambodian NGO that has traditionally been very successful at fundraising in Australia, was in the news again after a former chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia, was found dead after being charged with possessing child abuse materials. Financial support for Sunrise Cambodia will reportedly continue.
Second, there is no demonstrable demand for technical assistance offices or social enterprises on a scale that may mop up excess NGO programs and human resources. To date, no evidence has emerged that presents a sensible business case for this model of transforming NGOs.
Third, blended finance models may be excellent for particular types of NGOs, such as larger organizations working in agriculture, water, sanitation and hygiene, and health. But it is not a suitable approach for smaller, grassroots NGOs and those that have adopted strong social welfare, human rights, and poverty alleviation mandates. Expectations of financial return sit awkwardly alongside such priorities.
Fourth, sharing of resources is laudable, but it will not magically make more funds appear. Local NGOs tend not to take the sort of decisive and strategic action that would support mergers, and there are simply no examples of local NGOs in Cambodia merging. Some, like the author, might wish to see the CCC and the NGO Forum on Cambodia merge and show other local NGOs how it can be done. However, this would require high levels of sustained support, including access to legal advice, and advice about governance and organizational structure, human resource management and change management, and program delivery, among other things.
It is unclear if international NGOs and other donors will have an interest in supporting local NGOs with such logistics when the prospect of a merger starts to become more real. Of course, international NGOs can and do rationalize themselves at scale – consider, for example, how Oxfam and ActionAid continue to consolidate administrative functions at regional levels, how Corus International formed, and how Save the Children absorbed Merlin – but this is not a pathway that is visible nor even conceivable to local actors. For the most part, merging is akin to death. Certainly, mergers are anathema to the idea that NGOs bring income and status to their founders and leaders.
A bigger and more important question is: are NGOs really worth saving? The answer to this is not straightforward. Let’s remember that NGOs are not the center of the civil society ecosystem in Cambodia. NGOs were imported by international donors and shaped in their own image. They have a short history and are not indigenous to Cambodia. The functional equivalent of Western-style civil society in Cambodia is the intersecting business and political networks and complex patron-client ties that dominate Cambodian society. NGOs have supplanted rather than augmented or strengthened local forms of organizing. Community members are unlikely to regard NGOs as capable of representing them. NGOs are attentive to what powerful actors such as international donors, the Cambodian government and, to a lesser degree, service users and community constituents expect of them, which means they are less adept at leading societal change on their own terms.
However, there are some NGOs that can be regarded as essential. NGOs that focus on human rights and advocacy such as Licadho, Equitable Cambodia, or COMFREL should be a priority for international donors, as it seems highly unlikely that they will secure sufficient income from local philanthropy or national government grants.
It is entirely possible that large numbers of NGOs have already collapsed. Informal advice is that many of the supposed 3,450 NGOs are no longer functioning but are either unable or unwilling to deregister themselves. The collapse of NGOs will thus remain largely invisible. The Cambodian government makes it difficult to deregister NGOs; there is no clear process for doing this. Moreover, it serves the government’s purposes to be able to point to a large number of NGOs as evidence of a supportive and enabling environment for civil society. This has the potential to deflect any criticism that may arise in response to further crackdowns on civil society.
What should we expect then? And what is to be done? It is true that the future is bleak and adaptation is required. The CPP has tried and tested strategies that have proven successful in exactly these types of situations. The trade union movement and media organizations have been undercut and diminished with the entry of government-supported institutions into their respective spaces. If the playbook is followed again, it seems likely that a rise in the number of government-organized NGOs (GONGOs) will also follow in Cambodia.
In this light, a more realistic roadmap for NGOs in Cambodia may involve calculated and conditional acceptance of the demise of NGOs. It may be appropriate to learn from the experiences of the trade union movement and media outlets. It could also be necessary to cede space to GONGOs and look for opportunities to collaborate with and strengthen them. In particular, this could involve working to transfer knowledge that has been accumulated by NGOs in recent decades – including the human resources that hold such knowledge – to the emerging GONGOs.
Finally, it may be necessary to return to older models of civil society that privilege hyper-local community-based care, perhaps linked to Buddhist pagodas or other community-based institutions. In particular, this could involve systematically transferring assets and other remaining resources held by NGOs to smaller community-based organizations in rural areas. Such organizations reportedly number about 25,000, or one per 724 Cambodians, which seems adequate for the task of providing a much-needed network of support for Cambodian families and community members.
From the early 1990s through the early 2010s, Cambodia hosted one of the most vibrant, generously funded, and unchecked civil society ecosystems in Southeast Asia. Former Prime Minister Hun Sen once famously referred to the country as a “heaven for NGOs.” And indeed, up to 6,100 registered non-government organizations (NGOs) and associations have been able to flourish, including about 3,450 NGOs and 2,650 other civil society associations. This number of NGOs is very high by global standards, by one count making up the second highest number per capita in the world after Rwanda.
A confluence of disasters has changed all that. The heyday for NGOs effectively started closing following the 2013 national elections, when the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP) faced a major electoral threat and began systematically dismantling the public sphere. Viewing NGOs as a vehicle for hostile foreign-backed “color revolutions,” the Cambodian government introduced a restrictive and controversial Law on Associations and Non-Governmental Organizations in 2015. It also began to use tax audits, lawsuits, and political pressure – such as monitoring or disturbing civil society meetings, refusing to give permission for activities, and other coercive tactics – to restrict the sector.
Not only are NGOs required to navigate a suspicious and unfriendly political environment, but they also face a critically strained financial environment. Recently, the international development landscape has endured its steepest funding decline on record. As global power relations go through a process of significant reconfiguration and Cambodia simultaneously moves toward graduating from Least Developed Country status in 2029, global official development aid has been dramatically curtailed. This is set to continue.
The dramatic reduction in funds has had a significant and increasing impact on Cambodia and its NGOs. Already 10 years have passed since funding for Cambodian NGOs reached its peak in 2016. A recent survey of civil society organizations in Cambodia revealed that 26 percent of NGOs say they are not financially viable beyond 2027. It is not unreasonable to suggest that only one in five NGOs may survive the next decade.
In response to this calamity, there have been calls to redesign the ecosystem of civil society in Cambodia. These are led by the Cooperation Committee of Cambodia (CCC), which serves as the professional association of NGOs. A roadmap prepared by the CCC points to how major transformation can be achieved. Options being considered include increased reliance on local philanthropy; the reinvention of NGOs as social enterprises or technical assistance offices; blended financing; increased sharing of resources and organizational infrastructure; and, if there is interest, mergers.
If undertaken, these initiatives would together mark a profound shift away from traditional NGO models toward leaner, more specialized structures grounded in local ownership.
First, local philanthropy is captured almost exclusively by the CPP and, for the purposes of making merit, by pagodas and other institutions associated with Buddhist practice. There is little appetite among everyday citizens for giving to NGOs, and it seems unreasonable to expect NGOs to try and compete with entrenched political parties and organized religion in their fundraising efforts. A notable exception to NGOs’ failure to inspire local giving is the Cambodian Red Cross, which is skilled at generating significant donations from wealthy individuals. While this is a large and prominent humanitarian organization in Cambodia specializing in disaster relief, it is also compromised by political entanglements – its president is Hun Sen’s wife Bun Rany – and is the recipient of questionable major donations.
In any event, international philanthropy sometimes funds the wrong things, as any effective altruist will tell you. Well-meaning donors tend to give to projects that look good or feel good, not necessarily those that do good. Just this week, Sunrise Cambodia, a Cambodian NGO that has traditionally been very successful at fundraising in Australia, was in the news again after a former chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered charity raising funds for Sunrise Cambodia, was found dead after being charged with possessing child abuse materials. Financial support for Sunrise Cambodia will reportedly continue.
Second, there is no demonstrable demand for technical assistance offices or social enterprises on a scale that may mop up excess NGO programs and human resources. To date, no evidence has emerged that presents a sensible business case for this model of transforming NGOs.
Third, blended finance models may be excellent for particular types of NGOs, such as larger organizations working in agriculture, water, sanitation and hygiene, and health. But it is not a suitable approach for smaller, grassroots NGOs and those that have adopted strong social welfare, human rights, and poverty alleviation mandates. Expectations of financial return sit awkwardly alongside such priorities.
articles.summary: Imported by international donors in the 1990s, NGOs have supplanted rather than strengthened local forms of political organizing.

articles.title: Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN
articles.full_text:
The creation of the body, which comes ahead of next month’s ASEAN Summit in Manila, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the bloc.
Myanmar’s empty seat, as seen during the 40th ASEAN Summit (Plenary Session) in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Nov. 11, 2022.
Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.
The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.
Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.
Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”
While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”
Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.

articles.title: Indonesian President Replaces Head of Disaster Management Agency
articles.full_text:
The move comes amid growing scrutiny of Jakarta’s response to the forest and peatland fires that have drastically reduced air quality across the region.
Haze obscures the skyline of Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Sep. 18, 2026.
Indonesia’s President ​Prabowo Subianto yesterday replaced the head of the country’s disaster management agency in a bid to restore confidence in the government’s ability to bring intensifying land and forest fires under control.
Lt.-Gen. Kristomei Sianturi, 50, was sworn in as the chief of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) at the State Palace in Jakarta, replacing Lt.-Gen. Suharyanto. Speaking after the ceremony, the two-star army general said that Prabowo had given him orders to move as quickly as possible to bring the fires under control.
“The directive is clear: keep pushing forward and start your duties promptly,” he said, according to Kompas. “The target is as soon as possible, because the people are already affected.”
Kristomei said that he would review the BNPB’s response procedures to ensure faster action during disasters and prevent avoidable deaths.
“Responsiveness must be measured in minutes, not hours. That is what we will evaluate going forward, so there are no more unnecessary casualties,” he said.
No official reason was given for Suharyanto’s replacement, but the change came a day after the outgoing BNPB chief’s younger brother was arrested over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds, the Straits Times reported. The Corruption Eradication Commission said that the investigation centers on BNPB’s ready-to-use emergency funds, which are used to meet urgent needs during disasters, but did not say whether money intended to fight the forest fires was misappropriated.
Kristomei’s appointment – the second major change to Prabowo’s cabinet since the appointment of a new foreign minister on October 1 – is also likely intended to reassure Indonesia’s neighbors that it remains committed to fighting the wildfires that are currently raging on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. The forest and peatland fires have created a thick toxic haze that has darkened the skies above Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Timor-Leste, Brunei, and parts of the Philippines, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
As the haze has persisted, Jakarta has become the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires, many of which Indonesian officials admit were lit deliberately to clear agricultural land. As I noted yesterday, Social media users in Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia have become increasingly angry at Jakarta’s response to the fires, with some Indonesian netizens even urging Singapore and Malaysia to impose sanctions on their own government.
Meanwhile, politicians in Malaysia have called for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government to lodge formal diplomatic complaints with Jakarta, and the country’s foreign minister said that he plans to raise the issue at an upcoming meeting of his ASEAN counterparts.
Yesterday, after air quality readings in some parts of Singapore reached the worst levels in more than a decade, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires in Indonesia.
“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and explore joint action with other countries,” he said on social media.
Under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, passed in 2014, Singaporean authorities can take legal action against companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in Singapore, even if their activities take place overseas. History suggests that Singapore will refrain from confronting Indonesia directly over the haze issue, but the fact that Wong raised the prospect of investigations is a sign of the government’s growing frustration with its large neighbor.
Indonesia has announced a number of other measures designed to combat the fires. Prabowo yesterday approved foreign assistance for its fire-fighting efforts, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said yesterday. “The president has also given his approval, and discussions are now underway at the technical level. In this case, the technical discussions are being handled by BNPB,” he said at a closed-door meeting.
“What we need to emphasize is that this is a matter of great seriousness and is receiving the President’s direct attention,” Arrmanatha said, although he did not specify which countries had offered assistance or what form the assistance would take.
Also yesterday, the BBC reported that aircraft were deployed to scatter pellets of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions most affected by the haze. Indonesian police have also named more than 200 people and nine companies as suspects in forest and land fire investigations across the country.
Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at the National Research and Innovation Agency, told the Straits Times that the fires had “damaged the government’s image” within ASEAN, and that the reappointment of the BNPB head was “certainly part of efforts to restore the government’s image domestically and internationally.”
One way or another, the current fires will come to an end. Whether Indonesia succeeds in winning back the confidence of its neighbors will also depend on whether it puts in place policies and structures that can prevent a recurrence of a similar crisis in future.
