articles.title: After 8 Months in Power, How Much Has the BNP Changed Bangladesh?
articles.full_text:
It remains to be seen how willing the new government is to change the institutions that it now controls.
Tarique Rahman takes the oath of office as Bangladesh’s prime minister at the National Parliament Complex, Dhaka, Bangladesh, Feb. 17, 2026.
Tarique Rahman had been Bangladesh’s prime minister for just 11 days when war broke out in the Middle East. He took office on February 17; on February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran. By March, disrupted fuel supplies had forced Bangladesh to introduce rationing, putting further pressure on its economy.
Eight months into Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) rule, the results are mixed. Remittances have risen and inflation has eased. But living costs keep rising, businesses remain cautious, and law and order remains a concern. Mob violence continues.
The government inherited serious problems, but its decisions also need to be examined. Constitutional reforms endorsed in a referendum alongside February’s national election remain under negotiation. New rights laws have drawn criticism for weakening independent oversight.
How far is the BNP willing to change the institutions it now controls? And are its decisions making people’s lives better, safer, and freer than before?
Law and order remains a concern eight months into BNP rule. According to monthly data from Bangladesh Police, the force registered fewer murder, robbery, and kidnapping cases between March and September than during the same months in 2025. Burglary cases, however, increased, while mob killings continued.
Police recorded 2,122 murder cases during these eight months, down from 2,317 a year earlier. Robbery cases fell from 1,159 to 1,077, while kidnapping cases declined slightly, from 628 to 618. Burglary cases rose from 1,796 to 2,022, an increase of nearly 13 percent.
The total number of registered cases increased by 14 percent, from 110,296 to 125,763. Narcotics cases accounted for about 90 percent of that increase, rising from 31,111 to 45,091. The increase alone cannot establish whether drug offenses became more common or police became more active in registering them.
Mob violence remained a serious concern. A comparison of cumulative reports from Ain o Salish Kendra, a human rights organization in Dhaka, gives a toll of 131 people killed in mob beatings between March and August 2026.
On April 11, a mob killed a Sufi spiritual leader in Kushtia’s Daulatpur upazila following allegations that he had insulted religion. His shrine was vandalized and set on fire. Media reports said law enforcement personnel were present but failed to control the attack.
Similar incidents occurred in Dhaka in September. On September 25, more than 200 masked attackers looted and demolished the Radda MCH-FP Center, a maternal and child healthcare facility in Dhaka. A preliminary police investigation found that officers were present but failed to stop the looting. 
A day later, hundreds of attackers stormed a property and vandalized content creator Salman Muqtadir’s studio. Police linked the attack to a land dispute involving the property owner.
Police officers themselves have also faced violence. In June, a mob assaulted two officers in Savar and freed a suspect. In July, three police officers were attacked in Kutubdia while taking a suspect into custody. On September 5, Special Branch Sub-Inspector Altaf Hossain was beaten to death in Savar. More recently, on October 10, a police inspector was seriously injured in an attack by muggers in Khulna.
The government says the police are recovering. On August 26, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed claimed that suspects in almost all criminal cases filed during the government’s first six months had been arrested within a reasonable time. He said the administration had inherited a fragile security situation and was working to improve police morale.
Extortion also remained a concern. Court records cited in media reporting show that 723 extortion cases were filed across 49 police stations in Dhaka between January and August, a period that includes several weeks before the BNP took office. 
Dr. Md Tawohidul Haque, an associate professor and crime analyst at the Institute of Social Welfare and Research, University of Dhaka, described the government’s law and order record as mixed. “We cannot say that there has been any significant improvement compared with the previous one and a half years. At the same time, we cannot say that the situation has deteriorated dramatically,” he told The Diplomat. 
Haque attributed the lack of progress partly to uneven enforcement and the government’s failure to control its own personnel: “Unless a political party takes a firm position against wrongdoing within its own ranks, the situation will not improve.”
Haque also questioned whom drug enforcement was reaching. While drug users, small retailers, and couriers faced arrest, he said, influential figures continued to benefit from political protection. “The real patrons and powerful figures behind the drug trade remain beyond the reach of the law,” he argued 
Addressing that protection would require deeper changes in policing. “The Bangladesh Police has still not been depoliticized,” Haque said. “Its internal structure also remains largely unchanged.”
Inflation eased during the BNP’s first months in office, but the improvement was uneven. In March, consumer prices were 8.71 percent higher than a year earlier. Inflation climbed to 9.42 percent in May before falling to 8.34 percent in September, barely below the 8.36 percent recorded in September 2025. Prices were still rising, adding to costs households had already absorbed.
Earnings offered little protection. In August, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ wage index rose by 8.05 percent, trailing inflation. The index covers selected lower-paid occupations, including agricultural laborers, construction workers, and transport workers. For these workers, the figures suggest that wages still bought less than a year earlier, despite the slowdown in price increases.
There was more encouraging news from Bangladeshis working abroad. Remittances reached $18.94 billion between March and August, up 13.1 percent from the same months in 2025, according to Bangladesh Bank. These inflows helped replenish foreign exchange reserves and supported families receiving money from overseas. The improvement continued a rise in remittances that had begun before the BNP took office.
Businesses remained cautious. Bankers interviewed by The Business Standard (TBS), a Bangladeshi daily, described weak demand, expensive borrowing and energy shortages. Sohail R. K. Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia, told TBS that factories had unused capacity, giving businesses little reason to invest in expansion. The return of an elected government has yet to produce a strong recovery in borrowing.
The government inherited much of this difficulty. Bangladesh Bank had maintained tight monetary policy, while loan defaults continued to constrain lending. Its July–December policy statement acknowledged that higher interest rates alone could not resolve inflation caused by problems in markets and supply chains. It also announced a 600 billion taka financing package for industry, agriculture, and smaller businesses.
Fuel costs brought another setback in September. The government raised diesel prices from 115 to 135 taka a liter as the Middle East conflict drove up international energy costs. The Energy Ministry said the increase was needed to reduce losses at the state petroleum corporation. For businesses and households, it threatened further increases in production and transport costs, making the recent easing of inflation harder to sustain.
The government is also struggling to fund its spending plans. Banik Barta, a Bangladeshi daily, reported that the record 9.38 trillion taka budget relies on collecting nearly 7 trillion taka in revenue. Yet collections are falling as economic activity slows. 
Citing National Board of Revenue sources, the newspaper said revenue in July–August stood at 518.9 billion taka, down from 547.7 billion a year earlier and 291.6 billion below the target for those two months. Meanwhile, higher energy import costs, subsidies, increased public sector salaries, and major project commitments are adding to expenditure.
Dr. Khondaker Golam Moazzem, an industrial economist, policy analyst, and president of the Knowledge Hub Institute, said that high inflation, weak growth, and rising unemployment pointed to economic stagnation. He argued that the government had shown too little interest in the structural reforms needed for recovery. “The problem is that the government does not have the revenue support required to finance these activities,” he told The Diplomat, referring to its expanding spending commitments.
Moazzem questioned the timing of salary increases for government employees and large projects that he believed could be postponed. One such example is the large expansion of Biman Bangladesh Airlines’ fleet. Its orders for 25 Boeing aircraft from the United States and 10 Airbus jets from the European Union would total 35 new aircraft, compared with its current fleet of just 19. Moazzem warned that without reforms to the airline’s management and service quality, the massive purchases could leave Biman with a long-term debt burden that would be difficult to service.
articles.summary: It remains to be seen how willing the new government is to change the institutions that it now controls.

articles.title: Clean Energy Must Avoid the Mistake of Overdependence
articles.full_text:
The world must diversify its energy dependence, not simply relocate it from the Middle East to China.
For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.
Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources. 
The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.
Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.
China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.
China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.
Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.
Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system. 
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.
The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.
Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult. 
A critical part of China’s advantage is manufacturing efficiency. The IEA attributed more than 40 percent of China’s battery cost edge over Europe to automation and efficiency. In critical mineral mining and refining, China’s position also rests on decades of accumulated processing capacity and a willingness to bear environmental costs that many other countries have been reluctant to accept. None of this can be replicated quickly.
China’s enormous investment and innovation in clean technology has helped drive down costs and accelerate deployment. Attempting to exclude China entirely would make the energy transition slower and more expensive. Interdependence is not the problem, and energy security has never required producing everything at home. It requires enough diversity that no single supplier can disrupt the system.
As with trade, the answer is not decoupling but diversification.
Countries should identify where domestic capacity is strategically necessary, build alternative sources of supply with allies and emerging markets, and continue trading and investing with China where it makes economic sense. 
It can be done, but it takes time, capital, and political will. Las Vegas-based MP Materials operates North America’s only rare earth mine of scale, producing more than 10 percent of global rare earth supply. The company is building heavy rare earth processing capacity and investing more than $1.25 billion in a magnet manufacturing campus. Importantly, its strategy is becoming international: in 2025, MP Materials, the U.S. government, and Saudi Arabia’s Maaden agreed to develop a Saudi rare earth refinery to supply rare earth oxides to U.S., Saudi, and allied manufacturers.
This one refinery is not, on its own, a solution, but it points to the kind of allied, government-supported investment in processing that rebalancing requires.
While the world will remain dependent upon fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, the diversification to clean energy will continue, and the stakes will rise as demand grows. The world should not spend decades reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern and Russian hydrocarbons only to discover that it has exchanged one form of strategic dependence for another – this time on China.
For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.
Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources. 
The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.
Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.
China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.
China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.
Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.
Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system. 
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.
The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.
Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult.
articles.summary: The world must diversify its energy dependence, not simply relocate it from the Middle East to China.

articles.title: Nepal Should Not Shoulder the Himalayan Climate Crisis Alone
articles.full_text:
“No matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.”
Have you wondered why the current global order expects frontline geographies to absorb the astronomical shocks of climate disasters entirely on their own, especially when those very states face the unprecedented brunt of a crisis born from a total failure of global collective action? Who funds the recovery when the baseline geography of a nation is structurally altered overnight, especially when the crisis is entirely outside of their own making?
Of course, Nepal’s civilizational history has been a long, adaptive iteration to deal with an unforgiving topography and the sheer gravity of terrains that constantly pull everything down. But the scale of what we saw on August 26, 2026 was entirely unprecedented. The staggering images of landscapes dissolving that looked like a terrifying sci-fi reel made rounds among global audiences, 
Seven weeks have passed since a massive rockslide detached from a high mountain face in northern Nepal’s Langtang Lirung massif, slamming into the glacial lake below and triggering a catastrophic debris torrent along the Rasuwa-Trishuli corridor. The mud remains heavy, unyielding, and thick with the wreckage of a singular, devastating event. Ever since that unimaginable disaster, Nepal has grappled with the heartbreaking loss of close to 1,500 lives. Thousands remain missing. And thousands more are desperately trying to rebuild their shattered lives from scratch.
The loss is vast. And that stretches far beyond human lives and the statistical tallies of washed-away bridges and infrastructural damages. Or of erased roads or buried houses.
Take the sudden megawatt loss of hydropower assets clustered along this single corridor, projects that were either already online delivering power or actively under construction. Cumulatively, this single cascading hazard knocked over 400 megawatts of clean energy offline in a single afternoon. This is a fundamental blow to a country that has courageously looked toward a future of 30,000 megawatts of clean energy capacity by the next decade. Crucially, much of that power was not meant for domestic consumption alone but was strategically destined to flow southward across the border to anchor the green transitions of our neighbors too. The disaster wiped out roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s total installed electrical capacity in a single afternoon; that does more than disrupt domestic energy equations. 
The damage also includes the immediate destruction of the primary cross-border trade artery to our northern neighbor, China, the vital and the nearest entry point for the electric vehicles driving Nepal’s national green transition. Against all conventional global assumptions, Nepal has emerged as a global leader in green mobility, with new passenger EV adoption skyrocketing past 75 percent as the nation aggressively pursues the goal of becoming a fully electric economy. These efforts have now been paralyzed.
Even more devastating is what this corridor represents to the human spirit, and to our resilient high mountain communities. The tragedy impacted the sacred artery for international pilgrims journeying toward the ancient Kailash-Mansarovar sanctuary, a landscape deeply revered across Hindu and Buddhist civilizations, and a legendary frontier of adventure for global explorers. Tragically, many of those currently dead or missing under the mud include these very pilgrims and tourists. 
By flattening connecting bridges, stranding cross-border travelers, and decimating localized ecotourism infrastructure, these disasters have dismantled the historic human and economic ties and spiritual sanctuary of the region that bind South Asian nations together, directly threatening the collective dream of an interconnected green grid.
Then came September. Then came October. And both months bought multi-front disasters that defied everything we thought we could predict.
In September, extreme late-monsoon saturation triggered massive landslides across multiple districts simultaneously, repeatedly snapping grid transmission lines and fracturing vital economic corridors just as fast as recovery teams could repair them. 
October stripped away any remaining illusion of predictability. On October 11, a morning landslide and the subsequent breach of the natural dam along the steep Budhigandaki River corridor in central Nepal, west of Kathmandu, did more than wash away roads. The landslide slammed directly into the construction site of the 341 MW plant down the valley, specifically engineered to run off the river’s natural flow and step in during our hours of highest electricity demand. While the major structure was not entirely wiped away, the impact leaves us with fundamental questions about systemic safety, early warning capabilities, and the steep costs of re-engineering our infrastructure for a volatile future. 
Ultimately, if these vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the cascading risks will not stop at our borders; they will inevitably strip the entire region of the very clean energy opportunities needed to power our collective green transition.
Nepal, of course, has a lot of serious reflection to do regarding its own development thinking; we are by no means oblivious to that. But the broader crisis remains clear, because no matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.
This gives immediate, painful validation to the warning delivered by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Addressing the international community, the prime minister laid bare a grim economic reality, warning that physical recovery from these escalating disasters could consume up to 10 percent of Nepal’s national GDP. For a nation that contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, isn’t this far more than a localized setback? Is it not a crushing, completely unjust financial penalty imposed by an unequal global architecture?
Why should a frontline nation independently underwrite the immense physical and financial risks of cross-border infrastructure that the entire subcontinent’s survival depends on? Rather than pointing fingers among ourselves, isn’t this a definitive wake-up call for all of us in the region to come together, align our strategies, and act as a unified front? If our collective green future is at stake, is this massive burden truly for Nepal to shoulder alone, or is it the ultimate test of shared regional solidarity and global accountability?

Will we once again be treated as a passive, flat statistic on a ledger, or as a living warning of what happens when climate shocks freeze a real-world green transition?

If a nation that did everything right, pioneering citizen-funded hydro-infrastructure and skyrocketing its EV adoption, can have its clean energy core paralyzed in a single afternoon, who is it that truly needs to change? Is it Nepal that must reshape its ambitions, or is it a broken global financial system that must finally overhaul its slow-moving bureaucracy before the millions who revere and depend on these ecosystems downstream pay the ultimate price?

articles.title: China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea
articles.full_text:
The rise of seabed mining will add new complexity to the South China Sea disputes.
In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox. 
By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension. 
As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.
The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials. 
That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.
That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security. 
China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench. 
Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power.

articles.title: Anas Alhajji on the Three Seas Crisis and the Race for Energy Dominance
articles.full_text:
Dr. Anas Alhajji joins host Tushar Shetty to examine how the Hormuz crisis is reshaping global energy markets – and the overlooked impact of the loss of Russian and Kazakh supply.
Dr. Anas Alhajji, managing partner at Energy Outlook Advisors and former chief economist of NGP Energy Capital Management, joins host Tushar Shetty to examine how the Hormuz crisis is reshaping global energy markets. We discuss why Brent and WTI understated the price shock in Asian markets, the role of insurers in halting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the crisis’s toll on traded helium, sulfur, and fertilizers, the overlooked loss of Russian and Kazakh supply in the Black Sea, why India’s cuts to Russian oil imports ended up benefiting China, and the spread of China’s national security approach to energy as countries turn to domestic sources.
For more in-depth analysis on South Asia, subscribe to the Beyond the Indus podcast on Spotify or Apple Podcasts, or follow us on YouTube for video episodes.

articles.title: ‘One Day at a Time’: Inside an IDP Camp in Myanmar, Survival Is a Daily Challenge
articles.full_text:
Some of those living in the Old Kran Khun camp were once well off. Now they forage in the fields and forests around the IDP camp for food and firewood.
Firewood put up for sale by a household in the Old Kran Khun Camp IDP camp in Ponnagyun Township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State.
Sam Sam burst into tears when asked to narrate the circumstances that compelled her to become an internally displaced person (IDP). She pointed to clothes and utensils in her single-room thatched hut, the only things she could carry while fleeing her village. Then, she pulled out a tattered photograph from a bag.
“This was our home,” she said, pointing to the sprawling house in the photograph. “I never imagined that we would end up at a refugee camp someday.”
On February 6, 2024, the Myanmar military torched Kyar Ma Thout village in Sittwe township in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. It has burned down several other settlements in the area in order to deprive the Arakan Army (AA) of a base in the city’s suburbs.
Sittwe, the capital of Rakhine State and a military hub that houses the Regional Operations Command (ROC), is among three of 17 townships in the state that remain under the military’s control. By emptying its suburbs, the military is hoping to secure its control of the city and surrounding areas.
When Kyar Ma Thout was burnt by the military, most of its 650 residents, including Sam Sam, her husband, and two children, fled for safety in the areas under the control of the AA. About a third of the village’s residents, including a sizable number of elderly and disabled people, settled in monasteries in Sittwe city.
Sam Sam and ten other families from Kyar Ma Thout landed at the Old Kran Khun IDP Camp in Ponnagyun township about 80 kilometers to the north of Sittwe. The township was captured by the AA in mid-March of 2024 after weeks of fierce fighting with the military.
Their journey to the camp was perilous and involved travelling on the Kaladan River as well. With the arrival of IDPs from Sittwe, the camp’s population swelled to 1,643.
Old Kran Khun camp is one of 93 IDP camps scattered across AA-held areas. An estimated 100,000 people live in these camps, as per data compiled by the AA’s political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA). Another 100,000 are sheltering in monasteries and in the homes of their relatives. Those numbers could not be confirmed independently.
On February 8 this year, I visited the Old Kran Khun camp located 150 meters north of the highway between Ponnagyun and Kyauktaw. The mood there was heavy with sorrow and quiet desperation. There were around 400 huts in the camp. These were cramped and identical shelters built of straw, bamboo, and tarpaulin. The IDPs staying here are struggling to cope with myriad problems, including the loss of their traditional livelihoods, neighborhood networks, and support systems.
Maung Tin Hla is an affluent businessman from Ma Jay Mying (Ward No. 3) in Sittwe city. He owned five acres of land on the city’s outskirts, which was cultivated throughout the year and provided him with additional income.
Since the military’s offensives were directed at villages surrounding Sittwe, Ma Jay Mying had little reason to believe that the gun would be pointed at households like his own that were inside the city. But everything changed on March 16, 2024, when the military began targeting some localities and burning houses inside Sittwe.
Several people were arrested on suspicion of being AA functionaries. “We heard that the Arakan Liberation Party, which has joined hands with the military, had provided the military with information about some households. And I got the feeling that my name was also on the list,” Maung Tin Hla recalled.
On March 17, Maung Tin Hla began frenzied preparations to leave the village around midnight after a young man in his mid-20s was killed by the military near his residence. He hit the escape trail to the AA’s area of control with his wife and son and seven bags containing gold ornaments, money, clothes, and utensils.
After a grueling 90-km journey that lasted five days, the family reached the IDP camp in Ponnagyun township. Maung Tin Hla then purchased materials needed to build a thatched hut to shelter his family. He then arranged for food and water in the camp.
“I had around 1 million kyats (around U.S. $476), but this lasted just for a month. Then we began selling the gold ornaments. Almost half of the total amount I brought from home has been exhausted,” Maung Tin Hla said. “We can last for another year by selling whatever is left.”
Fishermen among the IDPs have been catching fish from the nearby Kaladan River and selling them for a livelihood. Others gather firewood, bamboo, and vegetables from the hills, which they consume themselves or sell in the camp and neighboring villages. But Maung Tin Hla is neither a fisherman nor is he adept at climbing the hills to gather food and firewood. His wife is busy all day with household chores and takes care of their 7-year-old son, who is enrolled in Grade 1 at a school about 2 km from the camp.
“So far, I have not been able to identify any source of income that will sustain my family,” Maung Tin Hla said. He is keeping his “fingers crossed and is hopeful of returning home soon.”
There are many like Maung Tin Hla in the Old Kran Khun camp, who have similar riches-to-rags stories to share. Their houses were either burnt by the military or destroyed by shelling. Forced to flee their villages, they are now sheltering in the IDP camp and are foraging forests and hills for food and firewood.
The daily itinerary in the IDP camp is dictated by scarcity. Long before sunrise, residents begin preparations to search for food and livelihood. Many embark on an 8-km trek to the hills that lie to the west of the camp.  They return by noon with whatever vegetables and firewood they could lay their hands on.
For Maung Aye Tun and his 14-year-old son, going to the hills has been a daily routine ever since they arrived at the camp from Mrit Nar village in Sittwe township two years ago, after it was burned by the military. “The hills are getting depleted owing to the unrestrained scavenging by camp inmates over the past three years,” he lamented.
“Now more effort is required to gather vegetables and firewood compared to the situation two years ago.  We have to go deeper into the hills every day. And there is no certainty that the same quantity of food and firewood can be fetched daily,” Maung Aye Tun said. Alarmed over the rapid deforestation of the hills, the ULA imposed restrictions five months ago on logging.
The daily expenditure on food alone for Maung Aye Tun’s family of four, including his wife and two children, is around 60,000 kyats. But his daily income from selling vegetables and firewood sometimes does not exceed 10,000 kyats. Whatever is earned is mostly spent on buying foodgrains.
During the rainy season, which extends from April to September, the availability of food in the hills drops, and there is excess firewood in the camp but not enough buyers in the rest of the year. Almost every third hut in the camp has bundles of chopped logs placed at the entrance waiting to be sold.
Larger households are able to send some of their family members to markets in the neighboring villages, where the scope of selling commodities at a higher price is brighter. But there have been times when the markets remain shut for days on end after airstrikes or shelling in neighboring areas.  This has eaten into the income and reduced food consumption for every household.
During my stay at the Old Kran Khun IDP camp, I came across three households for whom two square meals per day or being able to add vegetables to rice was a luxury.
Oo Tin Nyunt (75) is a widow without children, who was displaced from Kran Daw village in Sittwe township when it was bulldozed and then torched by the military in August 2025. She reached the IDP camp with the assistance of her neighbors who were also headed to the same camp. Except for 80,000 kyats, Oo Tin Nyunt had nothing else that could have helped sustain her in the camp. She survived on donations from two NGOs and the ULA till the end of last year.
She is currently dependent on assistance from other households in the camp. She is too frail to gather food from the hills. Neither can she work as a daily wager.
When I asked her about her plans, Oo Tin Nyunt stared for a few seconds and then, with a smile, said: “It’s one day at a time for me. I don’t know what will happen tomorrow.”
articles.summary: Some of those living in the Old Kran Khun camp were once well off. Now they forage in the fields and forests around the IDP camp for food and firewood.

articles.title: Don’t Call It a Reset: The Modi-Xi Meeting Wasn’t a Turning Point
articles.full_text:
Both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved.
Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompted speculation that India and China are moving toward a reset. Some see an opening for rapprochement, while others attribute the renewed engagement to deteriorating India-U.S. relations. Both interpretations overstate the shift in bilateral ties. Xi’s visit was important, but it did not mark a turning point.
Xi came to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, which also gave him an opportunity to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi. India and China’s participation in BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests. India’s engagement within multilateral organizations is a longstanding feature of its foreign policy, and China has not been a decisive factor in that approach.
Since the 2020 Galwan clashes, India has sought to stabilize ties and manage differences with China. These efforts have gained momentum amid U.S President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia. Yet the reasons for renewed engagement with Beijing go beyond the state of India-U.S. relations.
The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences.
It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India’s approach to it has fundamentally changed.
The border remains the principal obstacle. China’s recent statement that it does not recognize the Union Territory of Ladakh underlined the depth of the disagreement. There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences.
The separate readouts issued after the Modi-Xi meeting offered further evidence of the distance between them. There was no joint statement. The Chinese readout included a reference to Tibet and Taiwan that was absent from the Indian account. Beijing described India as a partner, but the Indian readout did not use the same language. The differences in wording hardly suggest a shared political understanding.
Deteriorating India-U.S. relations and uncertainty over Washington’s commitment to Indo-Pacific security have shaped the circumstances in which New Delhi engages Beijing. But it would be a mistake to explain India’s China policy primarily through its relationship with the United States. India has its own reasons to avoid another border crisis, and its willingness to maintain dialogue with China predates the current difficulties with Washington.
The suggestion that worsening ties with the U.S. have left India isolated, or made the Indo-Pacific less relevant, also overlooks the agency of regional countries. Their security concerns remain, regardless of changes in Washington’s priorities. The U.S. remains important to collective regional security, but uncertainty over its commitments does not remove the need for cooperation among countries in the region. The more immediate concern for Washington is the effect of its policies on its credibility among regional allies and partners. If confidence in the U.S. weakens, the consequences could extend across the Indo-Pacific. 
India’s security interests do not begin and end with its relationship with the U.S. Even as ties with Washington come under strain, New Delhi must contend with its own regional challenges. This does not mean India and China will draw closer. New Delhi can manage relations with Beijing while reassessing its ties with Washington; neither relationship necessarily dictates the other. Efforts to manage differences with China are consistent with India’s longstanding approach of preserving options without compromising its security concerns.
China-India relations are still short of their pre-2020 status quo. Security cooperation is limited, and military exercises such as Hand-in-Hand remain suspended. The trust needed for closer cooperation has yet to be restored, and the prospects seem far-fetched for now. 
For India, the unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern. The Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future.
Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset.

articles.title: Japan’s Nuclear Revival Has a Trust Problem
articles.full_text:
Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has made it clear that the nuclear restart is part of the answer to Japan’s energy uncertainty, but questions remain about safety and accountability.
Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Nuclear Power Plant as viewed in 2014.
When Tokyo Electric Power Company (TEPCO) brought Unit 6 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa back online in January, it became the first TEPCO reactor to resume since the Fukushima Daiichi accident. An alarm halted the restart the next day; the unit resumed operation in February and entered commercial service in April. Unit 7 at Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, meanwhile, is not expected to restart before 2029–30, according to the EIA.
Clearly, the restart announcement in January was a bit of a false start. Still, the symbolism was unmistakable: The utility responsible for Fukushima is again operating a nuclear plant, the world’s largest by installed capacity.
The timing was also consequential. The Israeli-Japan strikes on Iran on February 28 and the resulting effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz exposed Japan’s reliance on imported energy. In 2025, the Middle East supplied 94 percent of Japan’s crude oil imports; 93 percent of the country’s crude imports passed through Hormuz, according to Reuters. 
Japan’s exposure to Hormuz through LNG is much smaller: around 6 percent of total LNG imports, according to IEEFA. Yet Japan imports more than 97 percent of the LNG it consumes, and LNG generates about a third of Japan’s electricity, according to the government’s 2025 energy overview. The Hormuz shock therefore mattered both as a direct risk to Japan’s oil supply and as the cause of higher global gas and electricity prices.
The International Energy Agency reported that Japanese wholesale spot electricity prices in the second quarter of 2026 were more than 30 percent higher year on year. Futures in mid-July pointed to prices in the second half of 2026 nearly 40 percent above the same period a year earlier. These are wholesale-market figures, not household bills, but they show how a disruption to a relatively small share of Japan’s direct LNG supply can still transmit through global markets.
Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has made it clear that the nuclear restart is part of the answer to Japan’s energy uncertainty. She said in March that the newly reopened Kashiwazaki-Kariwa Unit 6, combined with a temporary increase in coal-fired generation, could cut Japan’s LNG imports passing through Hormuz by about 40 percent. 
That logic extends beyond the Gulf. A country dependent on LNG imports for a large share of its electricity is exposed to disruptions elsewhere in the Indo-Pacific, including scenarios involving shipping routes around Taiwan or in the East China Sea. For example, Japan’s continued reliance on Russian LNG has become a problem. The Sakhalin-II supply relationship has become a question of energy security, diplomacy, and policy autonomy. 
The strategic case for nuclear power is therefore not just about decarbonization or energy bills. It is also about preserving Tokyo’s strategic autonomy by reducing its reliance on overseas energy providers. 
Japan’s nuclear energy targets remain well ahead of the fleet it can count on today. The government’s Seventh Strategic Energy Plan set a target for nuclear power to supply about 20 percent of electricity generation in fiscal year 2040. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimated that meeting that target would require up to 30 reactors in operation. As of September 16, the latest date on the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s operating-status register, 11 reactors were classified as “Operation.” 
On August 26, the Green Transformation Implementation Council adopted a package calling for the maximum use of nuclear power, with safety as a prerequisite, as NucNet reported. The plan set out plans to replace two to five reactors in the 2040s and a cumulative 11 to 14 by the 2050s, alongside investment in domestic supply chains for perovskite solar, next-generation geothermal, and offshore wind. 
As Reuters reported, specific measures, including legislative steps, are expected by year’s end. The package is therefore more than a statement of intent, but key details – including the specific sites for nuclear plants – remain to be worked out.
Japan’s government may have a sense of political urgency, but its nuclear companies still lack institutional credibility. In September, an independent inquiry found that Chubu Electric Power, which operates the Hamaoka Nuclear Power Plant in Shizuoka Prefecture, had selectively used seismic-wave data to keep its estimates within internal parameters, despite earlier internal reports of irregularities. The inquiry also found that senior management had pressed staff to restart the reactors as soon as possible, according to Reuters. In response, Chubu said it would withdraw its applications to restart Units 3 and 4 at Hamaoka, and that its president and chairman would resign.
The episode shows what can happen when the commercial and political pressure for speedy restarts overtakes the discipline of safety review. It also gives opponents of restarts a concrete reason to doubt assurances from both utilities and government. Chubu says it may reapply after restructuring its organization and processes. Before it does, the company must show that its internal controls can withstand pressure to produce a favorable answer. Japan’s nuclear regulator, in turn, must be able to demonstrate that review standards are applied independently and transparently.
Public opposition, especially at the local level, is a related issue. Niigata’s governor approved the restart of Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, but a survey conducted before that decision found 50 percent of residents supported restarting Unit 6 and 47 percent opposed it. Nearly 70 percent said they were concerned about TEPCO operating the reactor.
The governor’s approval came with demands for clear safety explanations, evacuation planning, road improvements, and continued monitoring of TEPCO. In other words, local acceptance will require continued action on TEPCO’s part. A serious incident, a poor safety disclosure, or another data scandal at any plant can shape public opinion across the country. 
Three tests will show whether Japan’s nuclear revival can provide a reliable source of energy – especially in large enough quantities to make a meaningful difference for Japan’s energy security. First, can the Nuclear Regulation Authority retain public credibility while the government presses for a faster energy transition? Second, can utilities with past governance failures repair their internal controls and earn the right to re-enter the review process? Third, will the August package’s promised legislation and funding arrive by year’s end, and will the longer-term replacement targets be matched by realistic project timetables and local consent?

articles.title: How Chinese Clean Tech Is Reshaping Ukraine’s Wartime Energy Security
articles.full_text:
Despite China’s close ties with Russia, Chinese solar energy technology is giving Ukraine badly needed energy resilience.
A worker on a cherry picker installs solar panels on a building in Kyiv, Ukraine, May 9, 2026.
Russia’s war against Ukraine has shown that energy security is no longer just about access to fuels, pipelines, and large power stations. It also depends on solar panels, batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that can keep homes, businesses, and critical services operating when the electricity grid is under attack.
Ironically, most of the equipment helping Ukraine keep the lights on comes from China.
Beijing has maintained close strategic ties with Russia. Yet through trade and global supply chains, Chinese-made clean energy technologies are helping Ukraine reduce the vulnerability created by Russian attacks on its energy system.
Russia’s attacks exposed the vulnerability of Ukraine’s highly centralized power system. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that around half of Ukraine’s generation capacity was occupied, damaged or destroyed during 2022-23, while around half of its large network substations were damaged by missiles and drones. After another wave of attacks in spring 2024, Ukraine lost a further 9 GW of generation capacity, leaving it with only around one-third of its pre-war capacity. On January 20, 2026, another major Russian attack on energy infrastructure left almost half of Kyiv without heat and power.
Such attacks turned Ukraine’s large, fixed energy assets into major points of vulnerability, making energy decentralization an increasingly important source of resilience. Consequently, there has been a resurgence of solar power in Ukraine. 
The country was already a significant solar market before Russia’s full-scale invasion, ranking ninth globally for new solar capacity addition in 2019. But deployment and trade collapsed after February 2022. Chinese module exports to Ukraine fell from 83.9 MW in February 2022 to just 7.5 MW in March, and totaled only 15.8 MW in 2023. 
Since then, the market has recovered. The Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that around 800 MW of solar was installed in 2024 and 1.5 GW in 2025. Businesses and households have been installing solar power to reduce their dependence on the grid. Distributed solar PV, often combined with battery storage, has therefore become an important part of Ukraine’s wartime energy security.
International organizations, such as the IEA and the Center for Strategic and International Studies, have recently examined Ukraine’s energy reconstruction, covering aspects such as decentralization, solar power, battery storage, financing, and electricity-market reform. However, these reports tell us remarkably little about the sources of the equipment needed for this transition.
In particular, the role of Chinese-made equipment in this shift has received much less attention. According to the IEA, China accounts for around 85 percent of global solar supply-chain production capacity and around 80 percent of lithium-ion battery production capacity. Its share in some specific segments is even higher – for example, China supplies around 95 percent of global PV wafer capacity.
Currently there is no authoritative estimate on the specific share of Chinese-made equipment in Ukraine’s solar and battery markets, not least because some products reach Ukraine through third countries, international procurement channels, and aid programs. Still, given China’s dominance of these supply chains, Chinese-made equipment is likely to have played an important role in Ukraine’s decentralized energy expansion and will probably continue to do so.
This raises an intriguing question. Does China’s position in these supply chains give Beijing significant leverage over Ukraine? Could China, particularly given its close relations with Russia, use access to clean energy equipment as a coercive geopolitical tool?
Supply chain concentration undoubtedly creates structural influence. But as I argued in an article in September 2025 in The Diplomat, it does not translate automatically into the kind of coercive power historically associated with oil and gas.
In Ukraine’s case, three factors are particularly relevant. 
First, clean energy equipment moves through complex international commercial networks. A substantial volume of Chinese products can reach Ukraine indirectly through third countries, distributors, international procurement, and aid programs. This makes it difficult for Beijing to control the ultimate destination or end user. Blocking such flows would require much wider restrictions and would be commercially and politically difficult.
Second, weaponizing clean-energy supply would impose considerable costs on China’s own industries. It could expose Chinese companies to greater regulatory and compliance risks while strengthening Western arguments for supply chain diversification, domestic manufacturing, and “friend-shoring.” In the long run, that could accelerate precisely the reduction in dependence that Chinese manufacturers would prefer to avoid.
Third, such restrictions would contradict Beijing’s stated approach to the Russia-Ukraine war. China has repeatedly called for promoting peace talks while maintaining civilian trade. Deliberately restricting technologies important to civilian electricity supply would be difficult to reconcile with that position and could carry diplomatic and reputational costs.
When it comes to clean energy, China’s industrial dominance does not necessarily translate into the ability to exercise political control. Global commercial networks can significantly constrain a government’s ability to determine where clean technologies ultimately go and how they are used.
A further question is how the Chinese government and Chinese companies might participate constructively in Ukraine’s ongoing energy transformation and eventual reconstruction.
The potential market is substantial. The IEA estimates that Ukraine would need to add around 4 GW of distributed solar PV each year through 2030 to build a more decentralized and secure electricity system while meeting its national energy and climate objectives. It would also require an additional 5.6 GW of battery energy capacity by 2030.
For Chinese companies, the opportunities extend beyond exporting more solar modules and batteries. There is considerable scope for cooperation in system integration, energy management, technology transfer, joint project development, local assembly and production, and operations and maintenance.
But such involvement would not be straightforward. Chinese firms would have to navigate wartime risks, technical standards, financing constraints, supply chain security screening, and an increasingly complex geopolitical environment. Companies seeking to participate will therefore need to create value locally, build trusted partnerships, and adapt to an institutional and regulatory environment, particularly as Ukraine becomes more deeply integrated into European energy markets.
Ukraine’s experience offers a broader lesson about the geopolitics of clean energy. Countries still need secure fuel supplies and reliable power grids, but they also need access to the equipment used to produce and store electricity locally. China’s lead in manufacturing gives it considerable influence, though not complete control. Once solar panels and batteries enter global trading networks, they can contribute to energy security in ways that go beyond the intentions or expectations of their country of origin.

It also depends on solar panels, batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that can keep homes, businesses, and critical services operating when the electricity grid is under attack.

articles.title: The Africa Pivot: India and Japan’s Quest for Critical Mineral Security
articles.full_text:
India and Japan are betting on Africa’s critical minerals as the two Asian powers explore joint investment to secure supplies and expand mining capabilities across Africa.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi welcomed Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sane to Hyderabad House, New Delhi, India, July 2, 2026.
A new axis is emerging in the global race for resources, and the Indian Ocean serves as a bridge. It is emerging as a critical corridor linking Africa’s mineral wealth to Asia’s industrial ambitions. Africa sits at one end of a strategic corridor, and its minerals are becoming the new terrain of strategic competition. 
The continent is home to critical minerals essential for the global energy transition, including 55 percent of the world’s cobalt, 47.65 percent of its manganese, 21.6 percent of its graphite, 5.9 percent of its copper, and 0.6 percent of its iron ore. Africa is already emerging as a priority in ongoing India-Japan discussions on economic security and supply chains and, as the India-Japan leaders’ recent summit and the subsequent India-Japan Joint Declaration on Economic Security Cooperation confirmed, it now sits squarely within the partnership’s formal architecture. Backed by the India-Japan Joint Economic Forum, a new JETRO strategic report, and renewed focus on the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), India and Japan are positioning themselves to deepen cooperation in critical minerals, digital infrastructure, healthcare, green energy, and resilient supply chains across the Global South, seeing it as an opportunity for the next phase of investment. At the heart of this push is Africa, where the race for critical minerals is reshaping economic partnerships into long-term strategic leverage.
Forging a Trilateral Partnership for Africa’s Critical Mineral Future
India and Japan recognize the world’s growing dependency on China for critical minerals. China controls roughly 90 percent of global rare-earth refining and has also achieved a monopolistic advantage in development aid programs in Africa. This realization comes at a time when the new Trump administration, through an executive order in January 2025, titled “Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid” has suspended all U.S. foreign development aid, putting several welfare projects for African nations at risk. Given this situation, African nations are eager to diversify their partnerships. 
In this context, India and Japan can step up to support Africa’s development in a sustainable manner. Institutional cooperation on Africa predates both the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) and the AAGC. In October 2010, India and Japan held their first Dialogue on Africa in Tokyo, launched after the Japanese foreign minister’s visit to India earlier that year. The dialogue sought to coordinate the two countries’ approaches to Africa amid China’s expanding presence, highlighting Japan’s financial resources and India’s capacity-building model.
However, a significant triangular relationship is reflected in an MoU signed in June 2025 between Pensana Plc and Toyota Tsusho for rare earth offtake. Toyota Tsusho, the trading arm of Japan’s Toyota Group, committed to offtaking up to 20,000 tonnes per year of mixed rare-earth carbonate from London-listed Pensana’s Longonjo mine in Angola, with processing at Toyotsu Rare Earths India (TREI) in Visakhapatnam before final delivery to Japanese magnet manufacturers. This represents a significant step in developing a global rare earth supply chain and strengthening and diversifying the broader rare earth value chain. 
Similarly, the Mozambique LNG project, worth roughly $20 billion and led by France’s TotalEnergies, includes two onshore trains capable of producing about 13 million tonnes per annum. India has been in talks with several African countries to acquire critical mineral blocks on a government-to-government basis. In August 2026, India resumed talks with Zambia to explore investment opportunities in copper and other critical minerals, as New Delhi looks increasingly overseas for raw materials to meet rising ​demand from its rapidly growing economy. In Africa, ​the Democratic Republic ⁠of Congo and Zambia in particular can play an important role in meeting India’s growing requirements for copper and cobalt. 
Africa has become a crucial partner given India’s need to diversify energy supply sources to achieve its renewable energy and electric vehicle (EV) goals and the government’s “mines-to-magnets” industrial push. With demand expected to rise nearly fourfold by 2030, and near-total import dependency on lithium and high-purity rare earths, securing diversified offshore supply has become a national-security calculation. India’s mission to build a sustainable future depends heavily on critical minerals. New Delhi’s approach is not built on “extractive models” but rather on long-term capacity building, skill development, and technology transfer to ensure that African countries develop a self-sustaining growth ecosystem. 
India’s historical ties, along with its experience in trade and project implementation in Africa, combined with Japan’s strengths in finance and quality infrastructure, can provide an alternative development model in Africa. Tokyo has also been working since the 2010 Chinese rare-earth embargo to engineer its way out of single-source dependency. Hence, this will be a model in which India serves as the industrial concentration and logistics hub for trade with Africa while Japan brings capital, standards, and processing technology.
From Architecture to Action: Making the India-Japan-Africa Partnership Work
The architecture of this partnership reflects solid progress, but design alone does not translate into delivery. While India wants to keep mineral processing at home, Africa, through the African Union’s Green Minerals Strategy and national plans, wants to keep it on the continent. Japan needs access to resources in both cases. 
The ultimate test of an India-Japan-Africa trilateral partnership will be its capacity to turn agreements into tangible projects while accommodating the distinct and sometimes competing priorities of all three partners. A Joint Working Group could help bridge ambition and delivery. With no formal group yet established, however, its ability to do so remains untested. 
Whether the existing efforts translate into concrete outcomes will depend on execution. This includes whether Japan’s commitment of 10 trillion yen ($68 billion) over a decade through the India-Japan Strategic Investment Pact of 2025, and the critical-mineral, green-ammonia, and pharmaceuticals priorities, convert into bankable third-country projects rather than another shared vision document. There is a deliberate attempt to re-anchor the India-Japan-Africa relationship in a more coherent institutional frame, routing this effort through FOIP rather than presenting Africa as a standalone strategy. In this framework, FOIP has become the umbrella vision under which Tokyo and New Delhi organize their joint external economic diplomacy, from Northeast India to the Indian Ocean to the African continent. 
Japanese capital, India’s industrial and digital capabilities, and Africa’s demographic and market potential are increasingly complementary rather than separate strengths. The strategic question is whether these strengths can be integrated into durable investment and supply-chain partnerships. The real opportunity is to turn that complementarity into an economic architecture, one that moves India-Japan ties beyond diplomatic alignment and toward strategic co-investment. Africa is emerging as the arena where India-Japan diplomatic convergence could acquire real commercial weight.
A new axis is emerging in the global race for resources, and the Indian Ocean serves as a bridge. It is emerging as a critical corridor linking Africa’s mineral wealth to Asia’s industrial ambitions. Africa sits at one end of a strategic corridor, and its minerals are becoming the new terrain of strategic competition.

At the heart of this push is Africa, where the race for critical minerals is reshaping economic partnerships into long-term strategic leverage.

India and Japan recognize the world’s growing dependency on China for critical minerals. This realization comes at a time when the new Trump administration, through an executive order in January 2025, titled “Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid” has suspended all U.S. foreign development aid, putting several welfare projects for African nations at risk. Given this situation, African nations are eager to diversify their partnerships.

articles.title: Maldives Opposition Eyes Sweeping Constitutional Overhaul
articles.full_text:
The MDP’s constitutional reform program calls for splitting the executive into two separate offices: head of state and head of government.
Former Maldivian President and current Chairman of the Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP) Mohamed Nasheed addresses the MDP’s fifth National Congress in Male, Maldives, on Oct. 1, 2026.
The Maldives’ main opposition party, the Maldivian Democratic Party (MDP), held its fifth National Congress from October 1 to 3.
The congress, which is the party’s highest decision-making body, adopted significant changes to the MDP’s internal structure. It abolished the posts of party president and vice president, consolidating leadership under the chairperson, a position currently held by former President Mohamed Nasheed. Yet its most consequential decision was the overwhelming endorsement, by 520 of the 563 delegates present, of a sweeping constitutional reform program titled Bodu Badhalu (meaning “Big Change” in Dhivehi).
Formally submitted by former Economic Development Minister Fayyaz Ismail, the program seeks to address perceived weaknesses in the constitution adopted during the country’s transition to multiparty democracy in 2008. It argues that, despite the formal separation of powers, the president can exercise excessive authority, particularly when backed by a parliamentary majority. It further contends that constitutional safeguards for fundamental rights, including freedoms of expression, assembly, and the press, offer inadequate protection against executive overreach.
To remedy this, its central proposal is to split the executive into two separate offices: head of state and head of government. The latter would be directly elected by voters in a national election but could be removed by parliament. The head of state would instead be appointed by a special assembly comprising parliamentarians and elected local councilors.
The program also proposes several changes to the legislature, including setting a fixed limit on parliamentary seats, whose number currently increases with population growth; introducing preferential voting; reserving seats for women; and exploring a bicameral system. Citizens would gain the power to recall elected officials, while the removal of Supreme Court judges would require approval through a public referendum. The program further proposes reforms to the appointment and oversight of independent constitutional bodies to reduce political interference.
Regardless of its merits or prospects for implementation, the program’s overwhelming endorsement marks a dramatic shift in the MDP’s internal politics. Most notably, it reflects Nasheed’s renewed grip on a party that, until recently, had treated him as a pariah. Although formally proposed by Fayyaz, the program also advances Nasheed’s longstanding ambition to change the Maldives’ system of government, an ambition he now pursues alongside Fayyaz, with whom he has forged an unlikely political alliance.
Nasheed has long championed a parliamentary system, having backed it unsuccessfully in a 2007 referendum before winning the presidency under the new constitution in 2008. Following his controversial ouster in 2012, he narrowly lost the disputed 2013 presidential election to Abdulla Yameen. A controversial terrorism conviction subsequently barred him from contesting the 2018 election, which was won instead by his erstwhile close ally Ibrahim Mohamed Solih. Nasheed went on to win a parliamentary seat in 2019 and became speaker, eyeing a return to executive power as prime minister under a parliamentary system.
However, Solih resisted Nasheed’s efforts to hold a referendum on replacing the presidential system with a parliamentary one. Nasheed sought to advance the proposal at the MDP’s fourth National Congress in August 2022 but faced opposition from Solih and Fayyaz, then party chairperson and economic development minister in Solih’s cabinet. Nasheed subsequently shelved the proposal.
Relations with the party deteriorated further after Nasheed challenged Solih during the MDP’s January 2023 presidential primary and lost. He subsequently vowed to “destroy” the MDP and left to join The Democrats, a new party formed by his loyalists. Ahead of the presidential runoff, The Democrats demanded a referendum on the system of government as a condition of their support. Although the MDP agreed to hold one after the election, The Democrats withheld their endorsement.
Following Solih’s defeat to current President Mohamed Muizzu, the MDP’s National Council voted overwhelmingly against a parliamentary system, reflecting widespread resentment toward Nasheed, whom many blamed for contributing to Solih’s electoral defeat.
Yet Nasheed has since made a remarkable political comeback, reclaiming leadership of the very party he once threatened to dismantle. After a two-year hiatus from Maldivian politics, during which he served as secretary general of the Climate Vulnerable Forum, he rejoined the MDP in 2025. Strikingly, his return to the party’s helm was aided by former Solih loyalists, most notably Fayyaz. It was Fayyaz’s resignation as chairperson that created the vacancy Nasheed subsequently contested.
For now, the partnership serves both men’s political ambitions, with Fayyaz having supported Nasheed’s return to the MDP leadership and Nasheed, in turn, backing Fayyaz’s presidential ambitions for 2028. Bodu Badhalu was unveiled in April 2026 as the centerpiece of Nasheed’s chairperson campaign. It culminated in his landslide victory over a Solih-backed candidate, reflecting a profound shift in the party’s internal balance of power. The congress’s subsequent endorsement of Bodu Badhalu demonstrates that Nasheed has, at least for now, brought the party behind his constitutional vision.
Although that vision differs significantly from the traditional Westminster-style parliamentary system Nasheed has long championed, it nevertheless offers him a potential path back to high office. While Nasheed has repeatedly pledged not to contest the presidency in 2028 and reaffirmed his support for Fayyaz, he has nonetheless expressed interest in serving as head of state under the proposed arrangement, with Fayyaz as head of government. The precise powers and titles of the two offices, however, remain unclear.
Whether their alliance will endure remains an open question. Nasheed’s previous partnership with Solih fractured once the latter secured the presidency and asserted his political independence from Nasheed. Although Fayyaz formally proposed Bodu Badhalu, he had previously opposed Nasheed’s efforts to amend the constitution, and his embrace of reform now serves the purpose of securing Nasheed’s support for his presidential bid. Should Fayyaz win the presidency, it is unclear why he would pursue reforms that could curtail his own powers and establish a rival center of authority.
Even if sincerely pursued, Bodu Badhalu faces several challenges. Fayyaz must first win a competitive MDP primary against contenders including former Foreign Minister Abdulla Shahid and former Vice President Faisal Naseem, who claims to have Solih’s backing (although earlier reports suggested Solih himself was considering a bid). Should another candidate secure the nomination, the congress’s endorsement offers no guarantee that the party would remain committed to the program.
Beyond the primary lies the 2028 presidential election. Even if the MDP returns to power, it would initially face a hostile parliament in which Muizzu’s People’s National Congress holds a two-thirds supermajority. The composition of the next parliament, to be elected in 2029, remains uncertain. Meanwhile, constitutional amendments require a three-quarters majority.
Public approval would present a further hurdle, as changes to the nature of presidential elections require a referendum. Indeed, despite commanding a parliamentary supermajority, President Mohamed Muizzu failed to secure public support for his own constitutional reform proposal in April 2026, when voters rejected his plan to merge presidential and parliamentary elections.
For now, Bodu Badhalu underscores Nasheed’s remarkable political comeback. Barely three years after vowing to dismantle the MDP, he has reclaimed its leadership and secured its backing for reforms that could return him to high office. The question remains whether he can translate that influence into electoral victory and bring the program to fruition.
